subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF GRAIN ON GREAT LAKES-REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under Standing Order 43, on a matter of deeply urgent and pressing necessity, namely, the continuance of the strike which has stopped much, if not all, shipping on the Great Lakes for wheat and other products and is costing an estimated $10 million a day.
The situation is worsening day by day as the shipping season approaches its end, and promises to be a body-blow of disaster for western farmers who are shocked by the failure of parliament to bring in legislation to end the strike, a measure overdue since its inception.
I would, therefore, move, seconded by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), that such measure should be introduced at once.

subsubtopic: BUS SERVICE IN NEWFOUNDLAND-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
In view of the fact that in July of 1976 the government arbitrarily removed the CN bus service in Newfoundland from the jurisdiction of the Newfoundland Public Utilities Commission and placed it under the Canadian Transport Commission, with the result that the CTC, completely captive to the CN and the Minister of Transport, permitted a fare increase of 15 per cent immediately, with a further 15 per cent in the
summer of 1977, and in view of the fact that the Sullivan commission of inquiry has found the CN roadcruiser service to be operating with old, unsuitable, totally inadequate equipment at fares far above what is reasonable, and recommends that fares remain at a lower level, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That the government direct CN to withdraw immediately its application for further increases totalling an average of 36 per cent to go into effect on November 1 and February 1, 1979, that the CN be reprimanded for unmitigated audacity and audacious effrontery, and that the government direct CN to accept the recommendations of the Sullivan commission for improvement in the bus services and for lower fares than would be payable for travelling similar distances on a trans-island train service, and that the government return regulatory control of the CN bus service in Newfoundland to the board of commissioners of the public utilities of Newfoundland.

FUNDING OF HOME INSULATION PROGRAM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:

In view of the fact that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has described this program, CHIP, as the key item in the government's energy conservation program, in view of the fact that the minister also stated that the program, if fully implemented, would save this country upwards of 50 million barrels of oil, and bearing in mind that energy conservation is no less important now than it was a year ago when the home insulation program was introduced, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on an urgent and important matter.
Considering that it would be in the best interest of our country to have a genuine merchant marine and since our commitments toward NATO impose upon us the obligation to have an adequate fleet of ships, that our dockyards operate below capacity and that a large number of workers in these dockyards are unemployed, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette):
That the House order that a special committee made up of representatives of the various parties in parliament be set up to consider carefully this serious naval deficiency so that the government could order the building of merchant ships and others which would likely give work to our workers on the dockyards and which would allow our dockyards to maintain a permanent state of competitiveness.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of national importance and urgency, under Standing Order 43, to deal with further examples of Post Office lock-outs.
Contrary to the orders of the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) last week, Mr. Jack Lindsay, the postmaster in my home town of Oakville, confirmed that he was forced to lock out postal workers, without pay, last Tuesday on orders from national Post Office headquarters. Despite this lock-out, all local postal employees returned to work on Wednesday as soon as back-to-work legislation came into effect.

That this House compliments the CUPW members in Oakville and elsewhere who are crossing illegal picket lines in order to adhere to the law of the land, and instructs the Postmaster General to compensate accordingly those Post Office employees who were locked out by the government without pay last week.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Acting Minister of Labour.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
I cannot quite understand the shouting across the floor of the House. Perhaps it is a natural inclination to disorderliness.
My question to the Acting Minister of Labour is the same question I put to him four days ago. I understand that he might now have an answer. Can the Acting Minister of Labour tell the House of Commons whether he has named a mediator-arbitrator in the postal dispute, who that person is, whether there has been consultation with CUPW, and whether CUPW is prepared to work with that arbitrator?

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Acting Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to report to the House that I have appointed Mr. Lucien Tremblay, former chief justice of the court of appeal of Quebec, as mediator-arbitrator pursuant to Bill C-8.
In response to the question put by the Leader of the Opposition, the consultation process took place during the weekend. Not only was there consultation, but a last-ditch effort was also made to try to bring the two parties together and to convey the message to the union leaders that they ought to respect the law of the land, that no one should disobey the law of the land, and that they ought to encourage their membership to go back to work.
In a spirit of co-operation, the government was ready to start constructive negotiations immediately during the weekend. Unfortunately, these efforts were not successful and I indicated this morning, in meeting the union leaders, that I had no choice but to appoint immediately a mediator-arbitrator pursuant to Bill C-8.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can certainly express the pleasure on this side of the House that the Acting Minister of Labour,
Oral Questions
who promised a week ago that he would name an arbitrator-mediator within hours, has now-some six days later-been able to make that appointment.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
I would like the Acting Minister of Labour to either confirm or set the record straight on a news report by the Canadian Press this morning, quoting the minister as saying:
There can be no negotiations until the union obeys the back-to-work order passed last week by parliament.
That statement, if it is correct, would appear to conflict quite directly with section 6(l)(a) of Bill C-8 passed by this parliament, which instructed the mediator to proceed forthwith with his negotiations.
Can the Acting Minister of Labour tell the House of Commons whether it is the position of the government that the members of CUPW must obey the law before the mediator begins his work?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
If the Leader of the Opposition would look at the law, he would realize that under the law the mediator-arbitrator has a role to play. The law does not specify that he has to start immediately, but to start at a time which in his judgment is appropriate for him to do active and useful work.
I think the Leader of the Opposition is trying to play it on both sides of the fence. I suppose it is easy for the Leader of the Opposition to do this: it is easy to criticize. But basically what he should remember is that he would have been the first to complain to me if we had rushed into appointing someone without allowing time for some consultations and a genuine effort to pass the message across to the union leader that the union should respect the law and should sit down and work constructively with the government team, under the assistance of the mediator-arbitrator.

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE

subsubtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MEDIATOR-ARBITRATOR IN LABOUR DISPUTE

With reference to the mediator-arbitrator, it says:
-who shall (a) forthwith-
That means immediately -endeavour to mediate all matters-
I ask the Acting Minister of Labour a simple question: has he instructed his mediator-arbitrator, as is indicated by the Canadian Press report this morning, that no mediation is to continue-in other words, that he is not to begin forthwith, but that mediation is to proceed only if members of CUPW have first agreed to obey the law?

speakerposition: subtopic
Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice. At 12.01 a.m. last Thursday legislation was passed and proclaimed respecting the restoration of service within the Post Office. As of today, we do not have full and normal service within the Post Office. On Friday I asked the minister a question respecting the remedy of dismissal and he indicated to me in his answer that that remedy was subject to a great deal of difficulty as to its application by the government.
It is important for the House and Canadians to understand just what remedies are available: we should know what remedies are available to the government, in view of the open defiance by CUPW of the law of the land. Is the minister prepared to make a statement on motions later today in order to indicate to the House and the country the view of the

government as to what its remedies are in this situation? Regarding the obeying of the law, this situation seems to be reaching an impasse.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport and Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary for the Minister of Justice, or indeed anyone else, to make legal statements in the House as to what rights are and what the law is, in an elaborate way. Certainly, from time to time announcements may be made and decisions may be taken about such things as dismissals, but those are not under the authority of the Minister of Justice; rather, they are under the authority of the appropriate department, department head and minister.
As far as the current postal situation is concerned, clearly there are a number of remedies available. No doubt the public is interested in them. They include injunctions, and we are seeking those. We obtained some this morning in various locations. Also, there are various procedures by way of prosecution which are available to us. I think there is easy misunderstanding in the public mind that these prosecutions may follow very readily, simply because everyone in the public knows that these offences are being committed. That is an easy conclusion. But for the purposes of law enforcement, an attorney general must take care to ensure that the facts and evidence to ground a prosecution before the courts, and not in the media, are available.
That is what we are in the process of doing. I think it is important to say that that evidence, simply because we are in a strike and postal services are halted, should not be obtained in any careless or hasty way. In these cases, ordinarily we study the situation thoroughly in order to safeguard the liberty of the subject. This evidence is being obtained, the charges will be laid based on that evidence and those charges will be pursued to a conclusion before and under the law, regardless of the outcome or stage of a particular dispute. It is a matter of an offence against the law of Canada. Those who have offended will be charged on the basis of adequate evidence, and those charges will be completed.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is because of the importance of the public knowing what the position is that I invited the minister to make a statement on motions.
There is another problem relating to the law and its enforcement respecting those within CUPW who want to obey the law and go back to work. Aside from the injunction proceedings about which the minister must have some reservations, can he indicate to the House what steps he and the government are prepared to take to ensure that the people within CUPW who want to go back, do their job and obey the law passed by parliament last week will have the opportunity to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been, as has the Post Office, urging the return of these various employees to work, assuring them of every possible protection in the exercise of
October 23, 1978

what is now their legal duty. That is the position we have been taking and will continue to take.

speakerposition: subtopic
Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: REASON FOR REDUCED BUDGET OF DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. In the recently announced cutbacks by the federal government, the average cutback for most departments was around 4 per cent but the cutback in the Department of Agriculture was about 8 per cent.
I would ask the minister why he took such a heavy meat axe to the Department of Agriculture, because many valuable programs such as the Farm Credit Corporation program are helping farmers but they will now be severely hampered by this severe cutback.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: REASON FOR REDUCED BUDGET OF DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you segregated the reduction in the capital advance to the Farm Credit Corporation, the percentage reduction to which the hon. member refers would be considerably reduced. The reduction in the advance from the consolidated revenue fund to that Crown corporation does not necessarily mean any diminution in the efforts of that corporation on behalf of farmers: there are other methods that can be followed.
In so far as the selection of programs is concerned, Mr. Speaker, this was not an across-the-board percentage reduction by any department, and the average the hon. member mentioned is simply that, a statistical average. The choice of reductions was based on an assessment of programs starting with those that were considered to lack some degree of acceptable efficiency, and moving to those that might have been quite efficiently run, but where the priorities of objectives were lower than we now thought necessary in terms of over-all reduction in respect of reordering the funds freed up. That was the general process by which these were decided. The Department of Agriculture I think fared just as well or just as badly as any other in that sense.

speakerposition: Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: REASON FOR REDUCED BUDGET OF DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Regardless of how it is put, Mr. Speaker, the department is still cut back by 8 per cent. I have here in my hands a cabinet document dated June 29 and signed by a senior official in the Treasury Board. It indicates that the Treasury Board had recommended or authorized that the Department of Agriculture, namely, the minister, should discuss with the provinces two new agricultural programs, and the document went on to state:
No additional funds or man-years be committed by the federal government for the above mentioned programs until Agriculture Canada completes... its analysis evaluation of existing federal government programs currently estimated to be $ 1 billion per annum, and reports to cabinet as directed-

I would ask the President of the Treasury Board whether this total evaluation of federal Department of Agriculture programs referred to in this cabinet document is now completed and, if so, what are the results; if it has not been completed, what is the nature of the evaluation and are provincial governments being consulted?

subsubtopic: REASON FOR REDUCED BUDGET OF DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Minister of Labour. Given the fact that the expressed hope and optimism of the Minister of Transport for an early settlement of the Great Lakes labour dispute did not materialize over the weekend-the strike is now in its second week-and since it has been made clear by the Lake Carriers Association that unless a settlement is reached today, lay-offs will commence immediately, which will

speakeroldname: Hon. Andr6 Ouellet (Acting Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: MOVEMENT OF GRAIN ON GREAT LAKES-INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO END STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we had followed the view of the opposition, legislation would have been introduced last week which would have deprived the deck officers' union and management of arriving at a settlement. Indeed, the negotiations that were carried out, allowed for a collective agreement for three years to be reached and signed by both parties.
It is true that discussions with the marine engineers are taking place at the present time. I asked for an update on the negotiations before coming to the House at two o'clock. Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Some days ago, at the earliest opportunity, I gave you notice of my wish to raise a question which I felt I should bring before the House as it seemed to me to touch upon parliamentary privilege. The incident involves the behaviour of the CBC in relation to a member of parliament, namely, myself. The CBC is a Crown corporation responsible to parliament. Crown corporations enjoy a wide measure of independence and freedom from government control, which is quite proper. This means, however, that they

must be accountable to parliament for their actions. Without parliamentary control and supervision their autonomy would be virtually total, and since they exist to serve the public interest, and incur vast public expenditures in the process, control by parliament, as I think all hon. members would agree, is absolutely vital.
On October 7 I appeared before the CRTC hearings to make an intervention relative to the CBC licence renewal application. CBC provided direct feed of these hearings to all cable systems across Canada via satellite.
I provided an advance copy of my remarks to the CBC president and vice president. When my turn came on the agenda, I was announced by Mr. Camu to be the next intervener. At that point the television screens in the West immediately went black with instantaneous supply of recorded music for the ten minute duration of my presentation. I have checked and there were no technical problems with the cable systems or telephone companies. I was told that the problem was at the source, namely, the CBC. In addition to this, if technology had been a problem the CBC has not seen fit to send me an explanation.
This is a very brief account of the incident which forms the subject of my complaint. I submit that the evidence of members of parliament at these hearings has a significance which is of some importance. It is certainly no less important than that of other witnesses, and may even have a special importance in view of parliament's unique responsibilities in overseeing the activities of the CBC. I believe I was the victim of a serious affront on the part of the CBC in my capacity as a member of parliament. 1 believe that the CRTC was similarly affronted, as in blacking out my evidence the CBC was impairing the coverage of the CRTC's hearings. I have written to the CRTC notifying them of this misadventure.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1978-79-80 MEASURE TO GRANT SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING POWER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to rise in this House since returning on October 10 to start this new session, and it is my first opportunity to make the observation that this is a government in chaos. It is a government that has lost control of its mandate to run the country.
We were told that it was important to bring the House back to face serious economic problems and economic legislation and the government's program for turning around the economy of the country. There is not a single economic bill on the order paper, however, nor is there any of the promised legislation for action that the government said was awaiting the recall of the House. There is not any of the promised legislation and action that the government said it was awaiting the recall of the House in order to deal with, put it in place, and get the economy rolling again. There are no economic bills. There are no references to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs of such things as the commodity tax or Bank Act, items which were not completed in the last session of this parliament and given as examples by this government of vital pieces of legislation which needed to be handled by this House.
We have been promised a budget for the latter part of November. However, before that budget this government has the colossal gall to bring in this bill asking for authority to borrow $17 billion. That is an incredible sum, totally incomprehensible.
We are not told what the money is required for, what government expenditures are going to be next year, what anticipated revenues will be next year, what the rates will be, and whether there will be increases or decreases in the taxes. We are told nothing.
This country, through this House, is given absolutely no information about the government's plans for next year, yet we are asked to give the government authority to plunge this country further into debt to the tune of $17 billion. Can you imagine an individual or corporation going to a bank and saying, "I would like to borrow some money. 1 would like a line of credit for a few tens or hundreds of thousands." The bank is likely to ask for what purpose. "Well, I can't tell you." The bank would ask how you are going to repay the loan. You would say, "I can't tell you for sure." When asked how are you going to spend the money you would reply, "I can't tell you that, but I ask you to give me this loan now because 1 need it, but I can't tell you for what." You would be thrown out on your ear. You would not get one red cent from that banker.

That is the situation here. This government is coming to this House and asking for authority to borrow $17 billion. We are asked to trust it in terms of why it is needed.
We have a trustee position with regard to the taxpayers of this country. We have been elected by our constituents to represent their interests. When the government asks that a debt be incurred on their behalf, we have a responsibility to ask for what purpose, and to deny that authority until such time as we have been told why. Anyone who does not live up to that responsibility is failing the taxpayers within his constituency.
We are told that this is an emergency and the government needs the borrowing authority now. Some emergency! Last Friday we were quite ready to vote on the amendment. Apparently the government was not. We had to endure the spectacle of the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) proving to this House and the country that he knows as much about economics as he does about law. He rambled on in such a manner, using up the allotted time so there would not be a vote on that day. That is an example of a government in a hurry to get things done and move on with the nation's business-the Solicitor General standing up in the House to kill time, trying to make it sound as though he knows something about economics.
We would be failing in our responsibility to pass this legislation without questioning. This is an incomprehensible sum, $17 billion. In order to get it down to something we can understand, I will refer to income tax statistics. There are approximately nine million taxpayer in this country. On a per capita basis, that represents $2,000 for each taxpayer. That is not per individual but per taxpayer in this country. In 1976, the last year for which figures are available, the total income tax collected from these nearly nine million taxpayers was only $13,808 million. We are being asked to authorize borrowing in excess of the total income tax collected in the last year for which data are available.
If anyone managed their business, home or private life in that manner, they would be bankrupt. That is precisely what this government is doing, bankrupting us. This is precisely what the world economic community is telling us in driving our dollar down to 84 cents. They are saying precisely the same thing to this government that a banker would say to you, or I if we walked in and said, "We want more money; don't ask us why; don't ask us how we are going to repay it; we don't know but we will figure it out, trust us."
This money, $17 billion, or $2,000 per taxpayer, means that the total debt endured by each taxpayer in Canada will be $10,000. Each and every taxpayer in this country will be in debt to the tune of $10,000. The interest on that debt is about 8 per cent. That means from now on each taxpayer in this country will pay $800 a year for interest on that debt. That is not paying off principle. That is just interest on the debt, $800 per taxpayer per year forever into the future, unless we find some way of paying off the debt.
We must remind ourselves that this money is not being used for capital expenditures. It is not an investment in a capital project which will yield some dividends and allow us to repay
October 23, 1978

the debt over a period of time. It is operating funds. This is like going to the bank and borrowing money to buy groceries. Household Finance would laugh in your face if you tried to borrow money in order to purchase groceries or pay rent, without offering a plausible story as to how you are going to repay the money.
That is what this government is asking this House to do. We do not know how this will be paid back. We do not know what growth it has planned for Canada next year and the year after. There is no indication of what tax rates will be in place or by what rate they expect revenues to grow.
We are told the government needs $17 billion to spend on operating expenditures. This is most irresponsible for any kind of operation that you can consider. As I say, if a family operated in that way, it would soon be bankrupt. Any business would certainly be bankrupt. Any banker approached to finance that kind of operation would laugh in your face.
To compound the insult to this House and the country, of the government asking for this $17 billion without any indication as to how it will be paid back, on March 16 last the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) came to this House and asked for authority to borrow $5 billion. He said, and I quote from page 3859 of Hansard:
The authority in this bill to borrow a further $5 billion, together with the unused portion of the $16 billion authority granted in March and December of 1977, should provide the government with sufficient borrowing powers to meet all cash requirements for the fiscal year 1978-79, and provide a margin as usual for contingencies.
In March the minister assured the House that an extra $5 billion in borrowing would look after everything for 1978-79, with a significant margin for contingencies. Now he produces a bill which calls for an extra $7 million of borrowing for fiscal year 1978-79-$10 billion is for fiscal 1979-80. There are only two possible explanations. One is that the minister misled the House last March and that the $5 million extra borrowing power called for at that time was not enough to look after the whole of the fiscal year 1978-79, and he knew it. The other is he was so widely out in his projection for cash requirements that he needed another $7 billion.
There are only two possible conclusions to be reached. The first is that the government was being dishonest, a possibility which has to be entertained because at that time it was looking for an election in June, or maybe in October at the latest, and if ministers' statements were not completely honest they probably would not be called upon to account for them. The second possibility, equally damaging, is that the minister was incompetent. Mr. Speaker, can you imagine estimates being so far out as to call for an additional $7 billion, a sum equivalent to half the total income tax collected? It means that the deficit for this year will be wildly in excess of the minister's earlier prediction of $11 billion, huge though that is in itself; it will be much greater than that if he really needs this extra $7 billion.
Things have got to the stage of being tragic. It is not just a question of being angered by this misrepresentation or
Borrowing Authority Act
incompetence on the part of the government. The people of Canada are facing a critical situation as a result of the kind of direction and management they are getting. It is truly a frightening thing to reflect that we have been misled by the Minister of Finance or, in the alternative, that the government is so incompetent in its estimates of its cash requirements and the economy as to require on extra $7 billion. Clearly, all this has to stop. It is essential that changes be made and be made quickly. Unless they are, we shall find ourselves in an indescribable economic mess.
The word "depression" is not too extreme to describe what might happen unless the situation is brought under control. The government must do something about the excessive spending habits which have been built up over the last ten years. The fact of the matter is that taxpayers are simply unwilling to pay the taxes necessary to sustain that kind of spending. This is not just a subjective evaluation; it is an assessment which can be backed up logically and analytically. The evidence that people have reached their limit in their willingness to pay taxes is everywhere.
Recently I read an article describing the growth in cash economy here in Canada. What is happening increasingly is that the cash economy as opposed to the monetary economy is growing rapidly. This shows that an awful lot of people have taken to using, in their business and personal transactions, cold cash which cannot be traced or taxed. It is estimated that the proportion of the economy directly affected is upwards of 35 per cent. In other words, 35 per cent of the economy is effectively beyond the tax system. The assessment is relatively simple to make because the Bank of Canada knows how much cash is in circulation and the amount is growing far more rapidly than would be dictated by normal economic growth. So there is widespread tax evasion by millions of Canadians who now prefer to deal in cash as opposed to taking part in transactions which can be traced and taxed. This is of enormous consequence. Millions of Canadians are saying, "I am paying too much, and rather than pay more I am willing to resort to the inconvenience of a 'sock under the bed' instead of following normal accounting procedures which the tax man can trace".
In addition, there is evidence everywhere of the growth of the barter economy. A dentist attends to the teeth of the carpenter's children and, in exchange, gets a new bar built in his rumpus room; the lawyer, in exchange for helping draw up a will, accepts a leg of beef from the farmer. Indeed, there are firms which have set themselves up in the barter business and which bring together people who have something to trade and who would like some other commodity or service in exchange. These firms are making a lot of money from people who want to take part in barter arrangements of this sort. And the customers are saying quite clearly, "We are paying too much in taxes and refuse to pay any more."
All this has serious consequences for Canadian society. There is only one recourse and it is to cut expenditure. Governments cannot raise taxes beyond the willingness of people to pay them; all they can do is run deficits, as has been

October 23, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
the case for so many years. But there is a limit to the amount we can borrow without bringing chaos to the capital market. One way out is for the government to borrow from the Bank of Canada, which gets the funds through printing money. Printing money leads to inflation; it is in essence a process of taxation since it debases the value of the money Canadians hold. And we all know the consequences of inflation, the damage it does to the economy. As I say, there is no alternative to these huge deficits than to cut expenditures.
We must also cut taxes. We must cut taxes because we are at the point at which a reduction in taxation would lead to the receipt of more revenue than would an increase in taxation. This may sound like a contradiction, but it is not. If we accept the premise that a tax rate of 100 per cent yields zero revenue to government because no one would produce anything which would be subject to taxation, then at some point there must be a point in the relationship between revenues and taxation at which revenues begin to decline, that is, at which a higher tax rate will serve only to reduce revenue. This thesis is a very elementary one but I do not think it is assailable from a logical point of view; it may be argued we are not yet at that point of the curve, but I believe the empirical evidence is that we are, and that a reduction in the tax rate will result in an increase in government revenue.
Anyone who claims that deducting mortgage interest, as proposed by my leader and my party, would reduce government revenues, is dead wrong. That would increase government revenues, but we cannot rely just on reduction of taxes to raise revenues. There has to be a reduction in expenditures as well, because spending has gone beyond what an economy can or is willing to support in a non-wartime period. The people of Canada have sent this message to the government. They sent this message loudly and clearly via Martin Goldfarb and Associates.
The government responded with its so-called expenditure cuts announced September 8 of this year. Were those cuts or were they not? A couple of things which stand out must be mentioned. One is that the cuts of $2.5 billion proposed were cuts from projected expenditures of $54.6 billion, or a 12 per cent increase. In other words, the projected increase in spending for next year, before these so-called cuts were announced, was to be 12 per cent, yet last February or March the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) presented spending estimates for this year which showed a 9 per cent increase, and he said the government would do better next year.
In February or March the President of the Treasury Board said that spending for next year would increase by less than 9 per cent. Later he said he would cut $2.5 billion from projected expenditure increases of 12 per cent. What are we supposed to believe?
Does the President of the Treasury Board think that we have short memories or that we will not go back and look at what he said last February or March? Or was he anticipating

that an election would come along and bail him out so that he would not have to account? He was either deceiving us last February or March, or these cuts are pure fiction, simply a rearrangement which has nothing to do with reality. I suspect that there is probably a little of each, although this is not the first time this minister has attempted to deceive the House with regard to the spending plans of the government. This afternoon in question period, when asked about cuts regarding the Farm Credit Corporation, the minister indicated that they are not cuts at all but just a bookkeeping change. He said that the Farm Credit Corporation will not get its cash from the government any more. He said it will go directly to the market place.
It makes no difference whether the money comes directly from the market place or from the government; that is still government spending. To call it anything else is pure, unadulterated flim-flam. Exactly the same thing was done with regard to the Export Development Corporation, the Federal Business Development Bank, and CMHC. If we add on the amount of money borrowed by these Crown corporations, spending would be in the vicinity of $1 billion more. The government claims to be spending $1 billion less when in fact only bookkeeping changes are taking place. All the government is doing is rearranging the books in such a way that, if a business were to do the same, the securities exchange commission would de-list that business's stock. Any self-respecting auditor would refuse to sign the books, yet the government does it time after time. That is incredibly irresponsible behaviour. The sooner we turf these rascals out, the better chance we have of turning the economy of this country around.
The first and most important thing in bringing spending under control is to be honest about the spending process. That was the advice of the C. D. Howe Research Institute in its 1975 policy review. Three years ago that institute recognized that one of the reasons government spending has grown at the rate it has-and it has been allowed to grow at that rate-is fundamental dishonesty on the part of governments in presenting their spending plans.
First and foremost, there has to be more honesty about spending programs. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) should not be allowed to claim that he has cut the expenditures of the unemployment insurance program when in fact he has simply put some of the expenditures on the backs of employees and employers as they make their contributions. That is not a cut in government spending. It is movement of taxes from one place to another. The Minister of Employment and Immigration is not the only one who does that. Every ministry is doing the same thing. There has to be honesty about the spending process, as well as a willingness to make genuine cuts.
Is there a business, individual, or corporation which cannot find flab amounting to 5 per cent? Of course 5 per cent of fat could be cut without doing any harm. A cut of 5 per cent in government expenditures-a very small amount-would reduce expenditures by over $2.5 billion. The cost of sustaining that kind of debt is about $200 million a year. A 5 per cent cut
October 23, 1978

in the fat-not the muscle, the bone or the gristle-would reduce government spending by $2.5 billion and the amount Canadians have to pay in terms of interest on the national debt by $200 million a year.
Anyone with any degree of competence can find that kind of excess spending which can be cut. We were told earlier this year that a spot-check of civil service positions showed that 16 per cent of civil service positions was over-classified, that is, 16 per cent of civil servants are getting paid for jobs of a higher level than the jobs they are actually doing. The cost of that alone was estimated to be in the order of $175 million. Our economy is as bad today as it has been in recent history, certainly since the depression.

That is what the world is telling us. That is why our dollar is valued at 84 cents American. The world financial community is giving us the same message it gave New York city a few years ago. We are being told to bring our spending under control and to bring our revenue figures closer to our expenditure figures or else the world financial community will have to charge us much more in our dealings and loans. That is why the Canadian dollar is discounted to 84 cents American. If we had the healthy economy which we have the potential to have, our dollar would be worth much more than 84 cents American. That is the clear message.
We cannot bring our economy into line without first cutting expenditures. We must cut back on the horrendous growth in spending on the part of this government. We must cut that fat, not just because we cannot afford it but, in addition, people are becoming unwilling to pay taxes. We see growth in the cash economy to avoid taxes and growth in the barter economy to avoid taxes.
We see an increase in plain, ordinary tax evasion because the public sees how this government spends money. Any taxpayer who might feel a little bit of conscience or a little guilt about employing a tax-evasion scheme certainly loses that guilt when he finds out that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) spent $8,000 of that taxpayer's money flying his friends to a Grey Cup game, and that the Minister of Transport sent his nanny back to England on a government aircraft, and when he sees profligate waste and abuse of his money by this government. If anybody feels guilty about avoiding taxes, they will certainly lose their guilt quickly when they see the kinds of examples of abuse of trust placed in the government.
It is absolutely essential that government spending be reduced, that the tremendous waste be stopped. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie), last Thursday ran through a litany of examples of the government's abuse of the trust placed in it and the waste of our tax dollars. Those are not just little problems that are brought up for political advantage on a short-term basis. Those are very serious problems which have serious consequences on the attitudes of Canadians, their attitude towards paying taxes,
Borrowing Authority Act
the ability of this government to collect sufficient revenue to provide those services which are essential and to be able to close this gap between revenues and expenditures. Only when that is done, only when we have evidence that this government will be fiscally responsible, that it will treat taxpayers' money with the respect it deserves, should the House be asked to vote on whether this government should be given extended borrowing privileges. It is an insult to the House and to the country for the government to come to us now and ask us to authorize $17 billion in further borrowing, giving us absolutely no indication of what the money will be used for and where it is coming from. I, for one, will not abuse the trust of the people of Canada by approving of that kind of irresponsible behaviour.

Mr. Speaker, I will not continue speaking on this other than simply to say that what we listened to on Friday from members on the government side was two hours of concentrated bilge, twaddle and nonsense. I think my friend, the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), in describing the speech made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), expressed a very harsh criticism of the Solicitor General who, he said, knew as little about economics as he did about law. I consider that to be exceedingly harsh criticism and I hope that if, in the few remaining months during which this government is in power, it becomes necessary, as it probably will be, to have a new minister of finance, we are not inflicted with the disaster of the present Solicitor General becoming minister of finance, in light of the very reasonable assessment of his knowledge of economics made by the hon. member for Calgary Centre.
Another thing about this debate is the fact that there is such a bill. I think it has been mentioned by several members who participated in the debate that until November of 1977 the general attitude of this government was to tack on borrowing power to the supply bill, thereby depriving members of the House of the opportunity to debate this important issue. Last November, because we were debating income tax legislation,
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) tacked borrowing authority on to that legislation thereby enabling the House, at second reading and committee of the whole, to have discussion on the matter.
At the time the Minister of Finance admitted that what had been the practice heretofore was not a good practice because it deprived members of the House of the opportunity to discuss the question of borrowing authority, which is a very important privilege. It is not the granting of supply-we all admit that- but it connotes the granting of supply and it puts the government in the position-I intend to demonstrate this later-with the use of other powers, to be virtually given what is in effect supply. We had that debate and the Minister of Finance said in November of 1977 that he recognized the government had been depriving members of the House of the right, which they should have, to discuss the question of borrowing authority, and he would do something about it.
Then we come to March 1978. Because of a special agreement made among the House leaders to give effect to the urgent need of the government to borrow more money, a special order was made. We had two days of supply set back to back and in the second day-or the first day, I am not sure which it was-we had a bill with regard to supply and the question was debated with a time limit put on it. As has been said by my friend, the hon. member for York-Simcoe, by the hon. member for Calgary Centre and others, when we had that debate last March, the minister said-and I am simply quoting what has been put on record already, but it needs to be said over and over again, as reported at page 3859 of Hansard of March 16, 1978:
The authority in this bill to borrow a further $5 billion together with the unused portion of the $16 billion authority granted in March and December of 1977, should provide the government with sufficient borrowing powers to meet all cash requirements for the fiscal year 1978-79, and provide a margin as usual for contingencies.
Later on in the same speech, as reported at page 3860 of Hansard, the minister again said:
The unused part of the existing borrowing rights, and the new $5 billion authority requested will cover our domestic cash requirements in 1978-79, and will be used to draw on the $1.5 billion U.S. credit opening and the $750 million U.S. loan which is being negotiated.
I call the attention of the House to those statements which are clear, categorical assertions of fact. This parliament acts on behalf of the people and the taxpayers to grant supply and authority for borrowing to the government. There is a contractual relationship. When the government asks for supply, or indicates that it requires the authority to borrow money in order to implement supply, then certain categorical facts should be set before the House.
All of us are entitled to rely on the statements of the Minister of Finance as being accurate and factual. When the contract is broken, we must say to ourselves, "What will be the situation in the future? What about the requests for borrowing authority being made now? To what extent may we rely upon those?" This is far more important to the millions of taxpayers
October 23, 1978

outside the House, which taxpayers bear the burden of finding the money to pay the taxes needed to cover the borrowed moneys. They look to us to demand from the government the facts upon which the legislation is passed.
The reasons for the bill before us are very clear and simple. The hon. parliamentary secretary made a rather ridiculous point of order a little while ago. I admire him very much. Eventually he will learn what points of order are proper and what are not. I should like to refer to the comments of the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Martin) as reported at page 281 of Hansard dated October 19, 1978. He was referring to the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) when he made the following comment:
The hon. member knows this. He knows authority is being obtained now to cover the government's needs not only for the balance of the present fiscal year but for the next fiscal year so as to avoid our having to come back to parliament time and time again for the necessary legislation ...
That is the motto of hon. members opposite. They do not want to come back to parliament. They want us to grant wide powers respecting expenditures and borrowing money. They dislike parliament; it is alien to their method of government. They come here only because the constitution compels them.
The granting of a borrowing authority for the ensuing fiscal year would place us in a very dangerous situation. Together with the other powers the government possesses, and without bringing forward estimates or supply, the government is requesting a $10 billion borrowing power to cover estimates which have not been brought down. Apparently these funds are for certain programs which might be brought in next year. They are asking for a blank cheque.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre put his finger on it when he said that we are losing control of the opportunity and the power of challenging government spending, authority to borrow, authority respecting estimates, to act through orders in council and so on. That demonstrates the imperative, urgent and pressing need. There is no mechanism to make government appear before us to be challenged, of making it provide truthful information, or making the government justify its spending programs. That is the basis upon which this bill is being presented. Parliament, individuals, organizations, and the media do not have this power. In fact it is not within the four corners of the public service.
Once again I should like to refer to a rather fascinating story which I put on the record at the end of the last session. It concerns a very senior public servant in England who wrote a book entitled, "Your Disobedient Servant". Mr. Leslie Chapman wrote his book after resigning from the public service. He had been the regional director of the property services agency for the five southern countries in England. I hope the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan) will read my speech today, because he is interested in saving taxpayers' money. If he does not listen, at least he can read it later on.
This gentleman was able to institute savings within the four corners of his particular area of jurisdiction which amounted to 35 per cent. He had a spending program for property maintenance of 10.5 million pounds sterling. Approximately
Borrowing Authority Act
two or three years after the insitution of his program, he was able to show a reduction of 35 per cent of 3.5 million pounds. One would have thought that the senior officers of his department, the ministers and his colleagues, who were also regional directors, would have been interested in finding out how this reduction was accomplished. They should have been interested in what marvels this man exercised in order to save such an amount of money, without drawing blood and with the full approval of the involved unions. During the period of these reforms, he undertook consultation with the concerned unions.
They should have allowed him an opportunity to explain his program for the benefit of other departments. Instead of that, his colleagues disagreed and pooh-poohed it because they felt that the circumstances within his department did not exist in others. The permanent secretary, who is the equivalent of our deputy prime minister, said that he would take it under advisement, which is the usual guise. Nothing was done about it at all, and ultimately their public accounts committee got wind of the situation. That committee called a number of people before it, including the permanent secretary, for the purposes of obtaining evidence as to why no reasonable savings were possible within other departments. Subsequently, in approximately six months, the permanent secretary reappeared before the committee and admitted that he was wrong, that his previous statements were incorrect. By that time Mr. Chapman had resigned and had written his book. He explained thoroughly his experiences in the book. It should be required reading for all ministers of the government. I recommend it to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) as well as others. In fact I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will bring his mind down from the high, high clouds of constitutional problems and direct his attention to the simple, ordinary concerns of Canadians.
People are concerned with government expenditures and realize that there is a need for savings. The sequel to the story is that Mr. Chapman attempted to give evidence before the public accounts committee. But he was told that if he gave his story as an ex-employee or an ex-senior public servant of the government of England, he would be prosecuted under their Official Secrets Act.
That is what has happened, and that is why I said a little while ago it is useless to look within the four corners of the civil service for the kinds of savings that are possible, and I mean the simple, ordinary, homely savings which you and I, Mr. Speaker, realize in respect of our own households and our own businesses. A government adopting to its own use practices of this kind could successfully save lots of money without the necessity of decisions coming from the top that there will be a 20 per cent cut here, a 30 per cent cut there, and some 5,000 employees laid off. I am not talking about the merits of this, I am just talking about the way the government approaches it. I do not believe any of this in any event, and I do not think anybody else does.

To conclude this sad story of Leslie Chapman, "Your Disobedient Servant," I should just like to read two additional quotations from the book. The first appears at page 157, and is as follows:
There can be no shadow of doubt that the Official Secrets Act as it is at present worded and used contributes to the continuance of waste and extravagance on a massive scale in the public sector, and protects those who are responsible from the consequences of inefficiency, error and downright negligence.
That could be applied so aptly, so well, and so truthfully to this poor, shivering, frightened, weary and inefficient government.
Finally, the other quotation which appears at page 159 of the book, is as follows:
This book is concerned only with the financial consequences of unnecessary secrecy in the public sector, and there should be no room for misunderstanding on this point: while the Official Secrets Act is used as it is in this country, bungling and incompetence of all kinds can flourish undetected and the taxpayer will pay dearly for this.
That is the situation which exists in this government, and I know it as do you, Mr. Speaker, although you are in a neutral position and cannot make any comment. The ministers sitting opposite know, and the public at long last is beginning to know and to realize this, and will act accordingly as it did at the by-elections of a week ago. This is the situation and it is expressed in that particular act. We must find some better way of protecting the public in this regard.
Let us consider the period which led up to the situation bringing about this simple demand by the Minister of Finance in casually seeking authority to extend the government's borrowing power by $17 billion. During this period we saw program after program put together by government economists, political scientists and pseudo-experts, who all believe they really know better than the public itself what is best for the rest of us. Most of these programs were accepted gratefully by the executive as election bait, and with the massive propaganda machinery at the disposal of the government they were sold to the voters who were in fact being bribed with taxpayers' money, not realizing that they are one and the same person.
The result was inevitable. We were led to expect the impossible, and in doing so we bypassed the attainable. The grand masters of the Trudeau government, which manipulated this conspiracy of vast expenditures, now tell us that it was really the public which made these demands and the public will simply have to pay for them by massive use of the printing presses, which is what this bill is all about. We are told bluntly there is nothing we can do about it, particularly in parliament, except acquiesce.
As the rules stand now, that is the case. There is nothing we can do. We can make a few speeches, and government members are compelled by the rules to stay and listen to them. Members will blindly support the government when the bill comes to second reading, through committee, and third reading. The bill will go through, but there are other ways of dealing with this, and I referred to the by-elections as one.

In other parts of the world there have been attempts made by other governments to obtain the powers and authorities such as those this government is seeking. I am talking about proposition 13 in California. We have a parliamentary system. The question of referendum will likely be employed, or the government would like to employ it for its own purposes in connection with constitutional issues. For my own part I do not believe in it and I do not think it will work.
Flowever, I just want to say through you, Mr. Speaker, to hon. members opposite who sit there smiling, and I understand why they sit there and do not worry about this, that all over this continent there is a growing feeling of irritation, anger, discontent and challenge, not only in respect of governments but in respect of the whole machinery and process of governing, which includes legislatures, parliaments, and perhaps extending even to the media, so far as I know. This whole process is under challenge. I suggest very sincerely to my hon. friends that if measures of this kind and extravagant expenditures with no accounting, no truthfulness and no facts, continue by this and other governments, the public will seek and find other ways of dealing with the situation.
I agree with the late Sir Winston Churchill, that while there are defects in the system under which we operate, there has still been no better way yet found of bringing about an improvement over the parliamentary system. We can change and reform the system, but it is still the best system. 1 would like to see a solution.
I have been in this House perhaps too long, as some of my friends would say, during which time I have seen this happen over and over again. As I travel around this country I am convinced that the public, the taxpayers, the consumers, and the property owners will no longer tolerate, without some form of challenge, the situation that has been brought about.
Surely an example of this is the situation we are facing in respect of the postal strike, and the impunity with which, so far, the strikers have resisted this legislation. 1 am not on their side, and I am not going into the question of the law. We have passed this law and we cannot deal with it now, but when we pass a law there must be obedience to that law. If it is not a good law the remedy lies elsewhere in having it changed. However, the fact that there exists throughout this country now what is in fact a challenge to the power of this parliament and this government is a sure indication of how the people feel about parliament and about government.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance when speaking to this bill said that this House had approved the estimates and now had a responsibility to give the minister the power to borrow to cover the bill of payment. This, of course, is wrong so far as the fiscal year 1979-80 is concerned. 1 imagine the parliamentary secretary would now admit he was perhaps a little too enthusiastic in his statement and should have made a distinction.
As far as the fiscal year 1979-80 is concerned, we do not have the estimates as yet. The Treasury Board is probably dealing with those estimates now, trying to cut them down or add to them, as the case may be. We will know what they are
October 23, 1978

to be a little later on. This was pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe. In fact he is absolutely right in the sense that this parliament, this Elouse, which is presumed to be the caretaker of the public purse, is absolutely impotent to check or challenge the use of that purse, yet the minister comes before this House casually, almost in an impertinent way, with a short speech saying he wants this bill put through right away, "Hurry up, give me this borrowing power so I can take it to the Senate and get the money." In that way he is acting in accordance with the actual state of affairs in that this parliament in general, and this House in particular, are powerless to challenge the government's right in this regard.
We are impotent, not only because of the increase in tightening of party discipline, particularly on the government side, and a general unwillingness to challenge spending decisions made by government bureaucrats, who are not accountable to this House, but, as well, by reason of the extent to which this House in particular, and government in general, have given up all means of meeting this challenge. A very substantial part of the moneys which are spent, and which this borrowing power will be used to cover, ultimately is in the so-called statutory items which are held to be outside of our scope. I think it is a doubtful proposition, but it was a ruling from the Chair here in the past. I think that each vote in the estimates is a separate bill and can be challenged, but the rules are such that we cannot do it, and they are strictly enforced against us.
There are the debt charges and, the way the government is going with its borrowing, these are going to steadily escalate as taking a greater part of the tax dollar. That leaves approximately 30 per cent of the government spending, which may well be $53 billion this year, which lies within the competence of parliament and the right of the House to challenge. But even with that comparatively small percentage we have now powers to do it. By fiat, precedent and ruling in this House, coupled with the utterly hopeless system of examining estimates amounting to billions of dollars over the last decade or so, parliament has become a farce which, in fact, is a prologue to a tragedy. This is neither the time nor place to document this contention.
I do not think that there is a member of this House on either side who can stand up and honestly deny that public spending is and has been for years out of control, and this House can do nothing about it. The Auditor General has said that for a number of years. The last Auditor General has said that, and so has Mr. Lambert who heads the royal commission on accountability. It has been said by many people, and it was even said by a former minister on the government side, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell), while participating at the end of the debate on March 16, 1978, on the bill to which I have already made reference.
The hon. member said at page 3867 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to share in this expression of concern about the means at our disposal for the control of expenditures. I think it is a part of a general concern that has arisen over the complexity of legislation, the growth of
Borrowing Authority Act
the regulatory process, the growth and difficulty of managing expenditures. Along with the hon. member-
That is my colleague, the hon. member for Grenville-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker), who had the floor ahead of him.
-I want to say I share the expression of concern raised by the hon. member and hope that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) and his colleagues will give very serious thoughts to the concern we all feel, regardless of where we sit in this House.
I am awaiting hopefully for the Lambert commission to make a report. I hope and believe, from what was said by Mr. Lambert and his commission in the interim report, that they will deal with the question of accountability of the government to the House for its spending, or making known the information which this House needs to deal with those expenditures, and that they will make some very useful recommendations. However, it cannot stop there. I am hoping that this House will have the courage, determination, and grit to take hold of this issue and lay down some very strong recommendations so that the parliament which succeeds us will have an opportunity on behalf of the public to come to grips with this problem which, as my hon. friend from Calgary Centre has said, is on the verge of swallowing us.
No one can go on. If we were a private corporation we would be declared bankrupt and put in the hands of the receiver, but because we have the capacity to reach out and put our hands in the pockets of the taxpayer and come up with enough money, and enough bank credit by way of borrowing authority, we are not bankrupt. That is the only reason. It will not be the government that goes bankrupt; it will be the taxpayers of this country.
I hope that this parliament, now in its declining days, will render no greater service to the parliament which will succeed us than to call attention to this situation and make certain concrete, specific proposals that will permit that parliament, as trustees for the taxpayers and on behalf of the public, to challenge and properly scrutinize payment proposals and expenditures, so governments planning those payments will know that they will have to come and face a knowledgeable, determined House of Commons and Senate on both sides, and that their expenditures will be based accordingly.
There are two more short points I would like to make. I said earlier that I was concerned about the fact that the Minister of Finance had come to us on March 16 of this year and made a categorical assertion to the effect that the $5 billion borrowing authority then sought would be adequate, with a residue left over from the previous fiscal year, to complete all of the borrowing requirements for the fiscal year 1978-1979. That has not been the case, nor has there been an explanation for it. This is why I would hope, and I would think that it would be to the credit of this House and the government, that the government will provide that this bill, after second reading, would come into this House and committee of the whole, so there would be an opportunity for us to ask questions. Then the Minister of Finance, in full view of this House and the public, will come forth with reasons why, having made this statement in March, 1978, he is now coming before this House again in

The other thing which concerns me, Mr. Speaker, is the question of granting in advance the borrowing authority of $10 billion for the fiscal year 1979-1980. I would suggest as a possible scenario, especially to a government headed by a man who has not hesitated to use the War Measures Act and has indicated his willingness to take other unusual powers, that the right given by this parliament to the government to borrow $10 billion, coupled with the right which exists under the Financial Administration Act to govern by Governor General's warrants, would permit the government, for example, in December of this year or, better still, in March of next year, not to dissolve this House, but to adjourn it and govern for ten or 11 months without calling parliament together. That is the scenario which that particular authorization would permit.
I do not say that the government is intending to do such a thing. But we would be derelict in our duty to our constituents in asking them to vote for us as members of parliament with the responsibility to hold government accountable, if we had to admit to them shamefacedly that we gave the government authority to govern this country without the benefit of parliament for ten months. Once parliament has adjourned, it could use Governor General's warrants. I think this is an utterly impossible situation. I would vote against the bill in any event. Under no circumstances could I vote for it, and I hope that no hon. member will vote for a bill that would give this kind of blank cheque to this government. If one does, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that he deserves the confidence of his constituents.

They expected it would put forward the government's economic plans for the next six months, and that those economic plans would, first of all, bring some order into Canada's accounts and, second, would give us the economic thrust that all Canadians so desperately sought.
This throne speech came after a 100-day recess of this parliament. There was a president of the United States in the memory of all of us, Mr. Speaker, who talked about "100 days of decision". I thought that maybe during these 100 days of recess the government, not having to face parliament, would use the time to put forward an economic package that could be presented to this House, and through this House to the people of Canada, that would get the economy moving again.
