The hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell) frequently contributes from the back row, not standing up to make a speech. We expected for some time that this legislation would be forthcoming. It has cost the western grains business, which means the western Canadian farmer, some $10 million per day in lost sales. It is hoped we will be able to get shipping resumed on the Great Lakes in a day or two and that the government will be more successful in this respect than on the return of postal workers to their jobs.
As I was saying at the time of the intervention, just to give a symbol of the crisis management position the government is in I refer to what happened last week with the Canada Savings Bonds. Canada Savings Bonds, which is a major effort of the government to raise its capital needs, had an interest rate of 8.90 per cent. When the Bank of Canada raised the prime rate to 10 'A per cent, the government was forced to change the rate on Canada Savings Bonds to 9.25 per cent. That is just a symbol of this government's having to react on a day by day basis in order to keep the banker from locking the door on the Government of Canada. That is the stage to which we have come.
There was a general consensus in this House that the eight day throne speech debate should be suspended so we could proceed to economic legislation. That consensus seemed to carry right through the House. For two reasons the throne speech debate has been suspended: the first time was to pass legislation ordering postal workers back to work; the other time is this bill, C-7.
Canadians have the right to expect an economic package which would get the economic health of this country back to normal. Instead, what is the government's economic proposal? The economic proposal of this government in this time of crisis has been outlined by various speakers. It is an additional borrowing authority of $17 billion, $7 billion to be applied toward fiscal year 1978-79, and $10 billion for fiscal year 1979-80.
In 1946, immediately after World War II, this country had been through a period of great crisis, the war having followed immediately on the great depression. The accumulated national debt in 1946 was the same amount that the government is asking us to approve in Bill C-7. With the heritage we have received from those who have gone before us, those who built this country, this government is now asking for an additional $17 billion.

October 23, 1978
Borrowing Authority Act
That is a mind-boggling figure that I am not able to comprehend. This government asks for that amount of money without giving any explanation. Just this afternoon this government defeated an amendment moved by the official opposition which called for disclosure of the financial facts on the accounts of Canada prior to passage of second reading of this bill. We wanted to know why this money is needed, but what did this government do? It voted against an amendment which called for the facts.
This government continually postures that it is in favour of freedom of information. Every time the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and others like him bring forward legislation on freedom of information, the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) and his superiors rise to their feet and say that they are in favour of freedom of information. Once having said that, what do they do? They vote against it. They are in favour of freedom of information, but they want to be free to release to the Canadian people only that information which they feel is necessary. That is the kind of freedom of information in which they are interested.
What is this money to be used for? National debts can be accumulated generally for two reasons. Once, and it is valid, is to create a debt at periods of time when the nation's economy needs stimulus. The money is put into investments which will create jobs and long-term economic activity, not the short, stop-gap measures of which we see so many. Every member in this House in his private dealings has made those kinds of investments where moneys were borrowed and interest, paid to make an investment in order to enhance that individual's or his family's future. That is valid. However, what is this money for? This money is to pay for the ongoing operations of government. It is like asking your banker to give you a loan to pay for your groceries at a time when your bank account is in an overdraft position. That is what this government is asking.
This follows on the heels of a statement of March 1978 when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in this House on another borrowing authority bill asked for $5 billion for fiscal 1978-79. Others have placed this matter on the record prior to my speaking. He said that $5 billion would be all that he needed to carry the Government of Canada through to the end of fiscal 1978-79 and that it would take care of contingencies. That was in March 1978. Here we are, some scant ten days after this house has been recalled, and the government is asking for another $7 billion. Whom are we to believe? Are the people of Canada not to accept the words of the Minister of Finance?
I do not know if members if this House can grasp the meaning of $1 billion, much less $17 billion. In order to grasp what a billion dollars is, I did a bit of calculating. I want to show the magnitude of $1 billion. If from the day that Christ was bom you had spent $1,000 every day, seven days a week, every month of every year-and 1 think most Canadians can visualize $1,000-you would have spent $722 million. By the end of this century, you would have spent $730 million.
If you had had a billion dollars on the day that Christ was born and you spent $1,000 every day from that day forward, it

would be well into the twenty-first century before you spent the billion dollars. I have given the government the benefit of the doubt and have not charged interest on the $1 billion for over 2,000 years. If you charge interest, it would be a fund that you would never spend at $ 1,000 a day.
This government is asking for an additional $17 billion, but we are not to ask any questions as to how they are going to spend it. It is not our right to know. Mr. Speaker, we are members of parliament who represent the people, and we have a right to know. Does the government maintain that the people, through us, have no right to know? Does any member on that side want to go to the electorate and say: Vote for us but do not ask how we are spending the money? If anyone dares get up and make such a statement I will yield the floor immediately and allow him to do so.
To illustrate the seriousness of the situation in which we find ourselves, let me remind the House that on the basis of the minister's own figures the government deficit amounts to a billion dollars a month. It would take 200,000 years spending $1,000 a day to dispose of that amount of money, yet the hon. gentleman is able to show a deficit of that magnitude every month.
Canada may not be unique in the situation which has been created. Writing in the Washington Review, Richard Whelan outlined what, in his view, is the reason for the decline of the American dollar against other world currencies. According to him, when all is said and done you get down to one word, and that word is "confidence". The investment community, he says, has no confidence in the policies of the government so we have witnessed a slide of the U.S. dollar as against other world currencies. Mr. Speaker, if that is a slide, the Canadian dollar has been plummeting. Mr. Whelan writes:
The crisis the western democracies are facing is due to the fact that the governments of the west have not clearly told their electorates that the expectations which were coming forward could not be reached . . . The result has been the accumulation of deficits at a rate which few of us can comprehend.
All the manipulations of the Bank of Canada will not make up for the lack of that one ingredient-confidence. No matter who is governor of the Bank of Canada, no matter who is Minister of Finance, until the people of Canada have confidence in their government again we shall not be able to extricate ourselves from the economic morass in which we are floundering.
I believe there is another symptom of our present economic ills, and maybe many who sit in this House are not aware of it. But surely we are all conscious of the barrage of advertisements which come to our attention with respect to lotteries, whether regional, provincial or national. Lotteries have been set up as a supposedly painless method of taxation. All the statistics indicate that the people who buy lottery tickets most, as a proportion of the total population, are those in the lower income groups. These people, far from investing money which they can afford-if one could ever call lotteries an investment-are using money which should be going to provide essentials for their families. I know we cannot legislate ways in
October 23, 1978

which people should spend their money and I am not suggesting we should. What I am pointing out is that governments now look upon lotteries as a method of raising substantial amounts of revenue.
This is a further illustration of the serious economic state in which we find ourselves-governments resorting to schemes of this kind to pay for projects which should be legitimate objects of expenditure. Governments of all stripes and at all levels are beginning to think of lotteries as a painless way of raising money. I say this is a reflection of moral weakness. It is not my intention to create a straw man-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1978-79-80 MEASURE TO GRANT SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING POWER
speechtext: That is not a straw man; that is a villain.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1978-79-80 MEASURE TO GRANT SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING POWER
speechtext:
My hon. friend is correct. It is time for all of us to face hard facts. We must realize we cannot continue to carry on as we have been doing. It is not only the economists who are warning us, it is the so-called little people who have been saying to us: you had better be listening because we are fed up. Perhaps members on the government side did not get that message this summer, but as I went through my riding people were saying to me time after time: You fellows in Ottawa had better get your house in order. They know about proposition 13 and while they do not, perhaps, understand all the implications they do understand that the ordinary people in California had said "Enough". Indeed, in one of my smaller municipalities the people passed a petition based on proposition 13 calling on the municipal council and the school board to give account of their spending. After that, the taxpayers got the facts and went home. But here in this chamber we do not get the facts. We expect them from municipal bodies and school boards but we cannot get them from a government which states publicly that it is in favour of freedom of information and open administration.
There is one other aspect upon which I should like to comment briefly. The present situation has been described by some political scientists, philosophers and economists as a crisis of governability. While previous western democracies and their people had political differences, they had common goals, and while they might have had differences in terms of degree with regard to direction, they agreed on where they wanted to take their countries.
Theoreticians have started taking note of the present situation, as have many practising politicians who are eminently more qualified to speak on this topic than I am. For instance, Senator Moynihan from New York, who is not considered a conservative, argues that narrow interest groups in society have become so powerful and so self-serving and their own interests have become so dominant that they have lost sight of the common will and the common good. These special interest groups demand special treatment, and in their desire to win re-election, governments in western democracies accede to their demands. The only desire of this government is to cling to power by its fingernails, toenails and, as somebody said, its hangnails.
Borrowing Authority Act
Western democracies are becoming a little more than cheque-writing states. In other words, we come to the government and ask for more money, and we have the false notion that that will not cost us anything and that we will be ahead of the game. Even if that were true and not a myth, it would cost our children, grandchildren and great grandchildren. It goes well beyond the Biblical injunction that God would seek the sins of the fathers to the third and fourth generation. This sin goes much beyond that. When will it be repaid?
The result of contemporary states becoming cheque-writing institutions must be deficit budgeting because we must meet people's expectations. We cannot say no. Saying no is difficult. Saying no to our children is often difficult, but I submit that it is necessary, and it is time that we said no to this government until such time as it comes forward with information. The people of Canada should say no to this government until such time as they are given the information which they are entitled to expect. They should be given that information before they are asked to put on their children and future generations further debt amounting to $17 billion.
Small groups such as those I have described practise but another form of blackmail. That takes me directly back, in my closing remarks, to the blackmail perpetrated by this government. There is a form of blackmail inherent in Bill C-7. Hon. members on the government side might scoff at that, but how long will it take before some government spokesman will get up and say that we had better pass Bill C-7, because if we do not the government will not be able to pay for unemployment insurance cheques, the rightful pensions of senior citizens, family allowances and a myriad of other programs? That is blackmail of the worst kind. I am convinced that before too many days have passed this government will use that argument, because it has not been above using it before.
When I go to my banker hat in hand asking for a loan, he is gracious to me-at least he has been in the past-but he asks for certain facts. He wants to know if what I have in mind is a good investment, not only for the bank but also for me as a customer, because he wants to continue serving me as a customer. He wants to keep me in business. He is a builder and an investor. What does this government do? It tells the Canadian people that it will give no facts or information but that it wants authority to borrow $17 billion. If the government went to a banker with that attitude and with the debt portfolio it has, I wonder if, as the banker threw the government out the door, he would open the door first.
That is but half the story. The other half is that the government is asking for authority to borrow another $10 billion in 1979-80, without giving any information. We are not even being given information regarding 1978-79. The government is asking for borrowing authority for the future. Is that responsible? Can hon. members in this House responsibly support that kind of action? I say that it is time this government accepted the responsibility it has. If it does not, the fate which awaits it at the polls, of which it is so frightened, will surely come to pass.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on behalf of the hon. Acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet). He is necessarily somewhere else at this moment, but of course will join us as soon as possible.
The Bill is a very important one. The House has known that this situation was an important problem for some little time. I want to speak only briefly about it because I hope we have the spirit to move it forward as quickly as possible, yet, a few things need to be said about the bill.
Hon. members will not need to be told that I was very much aware, throughout the beginning of the strike and into its first days, that a strike such as this on the Great Lakes, involving the movement of shipping on our important inland waterway, could have very serious impact upon the economy of the country. I was troubled by that from the first, as many members of the House were. Yet there were other interests and questions at stake.
We have a legal system and understanding in which parties involved in collective bargaining have the right and obligation to attempt to arrive at an agreement between themselves. That
October 23, 1978

legal system allows for some help to be applied on their behalf through particularly the Department of Labour and its minister. That assistance was applied at various stages. In particular a conciliator was appointed. In due course he brought down his report, one which was not the basis for a settlement in the opinion of the parties. Thus, a breakdown occurred which led to the possibility of a strike.
I am sure Your Honour knows the law. We have collective bargaining. We have parties attempting to reach an agreement. When they fail to do so, the Minister of Labour may appoint a conciliator. When his report is in, it may be acceptable to the parties or not. If it is, clearly it is the basis of a settlement. If it is not, then after seven days the parties have the legal right to strike, to lock-out, to enter into a confrontation which is hurtful to them and unfortunately harmful to many other parties. Because it is harmful to many other parties, very often it is easy to ask immediately that the process be interrupted at the very beginning and that the strike be ended.
In this country, as in so many others, we have the right to strike. It was developed by labour unions forming and working together in the early days in conditions when it was a fight against oppression which led them to seek the right to strike and to fight. In those early days, typically the strike was illegal. In its beginnings it was by nature illegal, but it was resorted to because of the strong feelings of individuals that their rights were being overrun within our broad legal system.
In recent days I have had occasion to say a number of times that our democratic system depends not on sanctions and the power of the law so much as it depends upon the willingness of individuals, all citizens, to obey that law. That is a state of mind, a view and an attitude on the part of people which we must guard very zealously over time. The strike, illegal in its historic inception, became a legal weapon when it was recognized that alternatives were not easy to find. To this very day we have not yet found fully adequate alternatives to the weapon of the strike. Thus, we have maintained in our law, until such day as parliament assembled finds another way, collective bargaining, and the possibility of strike and lock-out if that bargaining fails.
In this particular case the bargaining failed; the assistance of the minister in the form of a conciliation report did not achieve an agreement; the parties stood apart and began a strike. Once again, the Minister of Labour intervened to bring mediation to bear and to recommence talks between the parties. Initially there were two unions involved in this matter and a single employer, and bargaining was ongoing with both. It was not easy bargaining. In the beginning, after the Minister of Labour brought them together one of the unions did not show up for the discussions. On the other hand, the Canadian Lake Carriers Association and the deck officers began their bargaining, and after a few days in fact did reach an agreement. Bargaining continued with the engineers who are involved in this particular legislation. As long as there was a chance of agreement without drastic harm being done to the country, it seemed correct in the public interest to let the
Shipping Continuation Act
bargaining continue in the hope of a solution being arrived at between the parties.
Of course, the problem and the danger to the country was growing. A short strike has less danger inherent in it because with the reserves of supplies, stockpiling, etc., the lack of movement of iron ore and other products would not immediately cause drastic unemployment and economic repercussions in the various industries. Even in the case of grain there is an advantage as long as the strike is short, so that grain could continue to move into Thunder Bay, our great terminal location for export to the east, and in its usual volume. Thunder Bay had been very low in stocks, and in the next few months we might have seen some problems in having enough stocks there to meet the exports we were trying to achieve. But as long as these stocks could arrive, we would have some catch-up potential, and the stocks would be there.
However, the day was coming when this situation would change. I was given the word today that this could happen in another day or so, and the movement of grain into Thunder Bay could not have continued as quickly as before. That we would have lost some movement into export temporarily is beyond a doubt. That is a price we pay for the collective bargaining process, with strike as a weapon in it. That is also undoubted.
Even today during the course of the question period the Acting Minister of Labour said that bargaining was continuing, and as long as it was, and he and I both knew that meant with any realistic hope of settlement, it was wise to wait a little longer. But an hour or two later we got word that the negotiations had, indeed, broken off, and that it now looked as though settlement was impossible. We immediately decided that the time had come to introduce legislation into the House and to seek approval of the House as quickly as possible in respect of that legislation. Once this step is taken, once a move in the House of Commons is chosen as the technique for settlement of the strike in place of the collective bargaining process, then surely the more quickly we act the better it must be.
We have presented to the House a bill which proposes a system for the ending of this strike immediately, and a manner of developing the collective bargaining agreement, the final agreement, between the parties. I urge members to support that bill. We will, indeed, in the course of the deliberations concerning the bill be proposing some amendments. I should say that some are simply clarifications, but others are to be proposed simply because the printed form of the bill could not contain them in light of the most recent developments which have occurred.
The one in particular to which I would refer hon. members is a proposal in connection with the clause concerning the term of the collective bargaining agreement, clause 4(1), in which the present term is indicated as continuing an agreement expiring on May 31, 1979. In light of the settlement between the same employer and the deck officers, it seems more

October 23, 1978
Shipping Continuation Act
appropriate to give the arbitrator the flexibility to take into account that settlement in full, including its term. Therefore, we will propose at the appropriate point to move an amendment which will allow the arbitrator to extend that term from June 1, 1979, to May 31, 1980. That is the term which is contained in the deck officers' agreement with the same employer. I think hon. members will appreciate the advantage of allowing that option to the arbitrator instead of confining him to the original straightforward year which was set out in the bill, and which had been developed, if not drafted in final form, before these latest developments had occurred.
It is not with gladness that we ever ask parliament in this way to end a strike, but with the feeling that the public interest will be served, recognizing the harm that might befall the economy if this strike continues-and some members will say too much harm has already befallen it-and recognizing also the importance of the collective bargaining vehicle and the need generally to have people in our society accepting that the law is moving when it ought to move and in a manner in which it ought to move.
I believe the very restraint in allowing the collective bargaining process to develop tends to assure that there will be compliance with this expression of parliament's will. That is extremely important. We know that in the face of another situation which demonstrates that, although people may all too easily think that the law can be a mechanism for causing certain things to happen, the law has its own limitations based upon our constant desire to respect the liberties of individuals and to assure that we move in a careful and guarded manner.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, with this indication of an intention to move an amendment in regard to term-and there will be a couple of others, but only in regard to language and the like- on behalf of the Acting Minister of Labour I am pleased to move second reading of this bill. I ask the House to consider it now, in all its stages if possible, as quickly as possible, so that since parliament has been asked to intervene we move quickly to put an end to this dispute.

Mr. Speaker, in rising tonight to answer the Minister of Transport and Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), and minister of other portfolios as well in the place of the Acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet), I must say-and I am sorry I have to say this-I have never in my life listened to a pack of sententious baloney such as we have just listened to tonight with the introduction of this piece of legislation. It may well be that the Acting Minister of Labour is late and is tied up somewhere else, and that does not surprise me a bit; but surely we should not have to listen to a professorial lecture on the collective bargaining system and why we now have to move, why nothing was done before, the fact that we do not have the structures in place to do anything better than what we are doing.
In this regard I would point to the fact that over the last decade there have been the recommendations of the Woods committee, recommendations that the Acting Minister of Labour told the Senate the other night are under active consideration, which the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Tru-

deau) later in this House of Commons denied. These have been things advocated by the official opposition for many years. For the minister to come into this House and tell us there is no better way, that this is the way we have to do it, is just too much for hon. members to have to listen to with any patience.
If I lose my patience at the beginning of my speech it is only because this long night, and it may be a long one, is going to require all of the rest of my patience-and I have a great deal-in order to see this bill through.

That is all it is. The government does not have anything to be very proud of tonight. We come here tonight less than one week after we passed a piece of legislation that has not been obeyed. We asked the government when they would appoint a mediator-arbitrator and we were told it would be within hours, but it was done only today. We were asked to pass this other piece of legislation because the public was entitled to mail service, but nearly everybody in the country knows that something much more substantive, intelligent and sophisticated should have been done many months ago.
Tonight we are suddenly asked to pass this legislation. We have listened to a lecture from the Minister of Justice, who is also the Minister of Transport and is speaking for the Acting Minister of Labour. We are asked to pass this legislation when the government does not even have a Minister of Labour. There is nothing personal in saying this, because the Acting Minister of Labour is working hard, but there is no permanent Minister of Labour. We are asked to go along with the government against a backdrop of back to work legislation that is being openly defied. The Minister of Justice has told us for several days that there are certain remedies available as against the postal workers, but he cannot seem to define what they are in terms of back to work steps or disciplinary action.
Against this entire backdrop, Mr. Speaker, we listened to this speech by the Minister of Justice, who told us that this is the only way things can be done. The fact is that if this is the only way things can be done, this House is going to become nothing but a tribunal for settling labour disputes. That is the very thing that all hon. members, if they are honest with each other, would say this House is incapable of being.
I and my party recognize that the situation we are in tonight is very serious. Winter is coming. When the minister said that action had to be taken, there is concurrence for that on this side of the House. Just the other day, however, in asking the minister why he was getting excited only now, if he had known for three months what the effect of a breakdown in the negotiations would be, he had no answer except to say that the government had been monitoring the situation closely and was fully aware of what the economic consequences would be. Yet the government says this is the only way we can proceed. It
October 23, 1978

rejects out of hand the recommendations of the Woods royal commission which years ago recognized that there has to be a better method.
In situations in which these disputes go down to the final crunch, as this one has tonight, hon. members are completely and utterly dependent on the information which the government gives them. It was obvious less than a week ago that the information hon. members were given upon which Bill C-8 was put through to reinstate postal service in this country was somewhat less than the calibre of accuracy that is demanded in this House.
We are in agreement with one thing the minister has said, and that is that we are facing serious economic loss. Some of the figures are worth relating. The Canadian Wheat Board is now behind over 3.5 to four million tonnes of grain which must be shipped before December 15. There is nearly $500 million in costs, and it has been estimated that if this grain does not go through before freeze-up the economic cost to the country will be approximately $1 billion. Producers are losing $10 million a day, and some ship owners say that they are facing losses of more than $200,000 a day.
It is not just a matter of economic loss. There are approximately 2,100 seamen who face being laid off. With an unemployment level of nearly one million in this country, this is not the time to be laying off another 2,100 people who have to support their families. The economic impact of this withdrawal of service is obvious to everyone, but what is hard to understand is why it has taken so long for the government of the day, a government that has been in power for over a decade, to recognize that this ad hoc method of dealing with such situations is not satisfactory, and, as we are finding out with the legislation we passed a week ago, it does not even work very well.
There are certain questions which must be asked tonight. My party will want to know before this legislation passes-and the minister cannot quarrel with us for asking these questions-if they actually have an arbitrator, a person who is prepared to act or who has given an undertaking to the government that he or she will act in this capacity. We will want to know whether there has been any discussion with the union involved as to whether or not the union executive and the rank and file of that union are prepared to obey the law. This country cannot tolerate two pieces of back to work legislation passed within the space of one week which are not going to be obeyed.
We would also like to know, Mr. Speaker, what is the assessment of damage which the minister referred to when I directed a question in this regard to him the other day. We want to hear more about this because one of the things that is essential for the public and the labour movement to understand is the economic assessment of the damages, information which the minister has said the government has.
We do not intend to throw procedural roadblocks in the way of this bill. It is too important to too many people and to the economy of Canada. But it is very strange to listen to the minister tell us tonight that when the government was asked in
Shipping Continuation Act
question period today whether they were going to introduce legislation, the answer was, "Not as long as negotiations are continuing." One would wonder whether the government in giving that answer was being somewhat less than frank with the opposition and with the public of Canada. The speed with which this bill was brought before the House makes us ask whether or not the government knew prior to question period today that there was no hope of negotiations continuing.
I want to emphasize that we will want satisfaction from the minister when it comes to committee of the whole. I know the minister will not object when I say that we want to be satisfied that there was no possibility of the negotiations continuing, that in fact there have been some commitments to the government that the law will be obeyed and that-and this is very important in view of the fact that the same is not happening in the postal strike-the government is in a position to back up the legislation.
Tonight the minister made much of the fact that the law must be accepted. That is true. In the long run, in a free community that is the only kind of law that will last. One of the things that decides whether the law is accepted is whether anybody can be sure it will be obeyed. We will want to be sure that this is not a toothless bill.
We intend to ask a lot of questions at committee of the whole, Mr. Speaker. We will not throw any procedural roadblocks in the way of the bill but we cannot help commenting that the present system of dealing with disputes of this kind is not satisfactory. We have advocated a better way but until the last few days the government, despite the fact they say they have been examining it, have rejected it. The proposals we put forward have the backing of a royal commission on labour-management relations in Canada.
We have had a decade of experience which indicates that this ad hoc method of dealing with matters is not satisfactory and does nothing to enhance labour relations. Indeed, every speech made by members of this government before they bring in legislation rescinding the right to withdraw services is preceded by the pious statement that the government believes in the right to free collective bargaining and the right to strike.

subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF SHIPPING SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the government proposes in this bill tonight is not simply to order some workers on the Great Lakes ships back to work. In effect, what the government is doing tonight and what it did a week ago is to destroy the fundamental principle of collective bargaining which has existed in this country for almost 50 years.
Back in the 1920s when that great Liberal leader, former prime minister, former friend and co-worker of the Rockefellers in the United States, and one of the original instigators of the notorious company unions, Mr. Mackenzie King, gave workers in Canada in the private sector the right to strike, it was more hedged around with rules, regulations and proce-

October 23, 1978
Shipping Continuation Act
dures than is the case with any other country in the democratic world.
It should be remembered that workers in the private sector of the economy who want to go on strike have to follow a very carefully constructed and elaborate set of procedures. They have to try to negotiate with their employers. If they cannot reach an agreement they have to ask for a conciliator appointed by the government. If the conciliator cannot bring the parties together, the government appoints a conciliation board with one representative of the union, one representative of the employers and a chairman who is either agreed upon by both parties or, if they cannot agree, is appointed by the government. Only after the conciliation board has made a report and recommendations, and only if members of the unions do not believe that the recommendations are adequate or if the company will not accept the report, can the workers decide on a legal strike. That has been the procedure for many, many years.
It was only in 1967 that workers in the private sector were given the right to collective bargaining. That right is embodied in the Public Service Staff Relations Act which had the approval of almost all the members of the political parties represented in the parliament of that time. The bill provided that government employees had the right to belong to unions of their choice, the right to bargain with their employer, the government, on many important issues, although it excluded some, and that they could in the course of their negotiations choose to reach a final settlement either by arbitration or by exercising their right to strike. In most cases the unions opted for arbitration as the final way of settling disputes with the government.
In the case of the postal workers, they opted for the right to strike. Last week we saw the postal workers, having bargained for some 18 months without reaching an agreement-indeed, having dozens if not hundreds of clauses in their agreement not settled-opting for the right to strike. I am not discussing whether their demands were exorbitant, but they were exercising the right the parliament of Canada had given them if they could not reach an agreement. On the first day of their strike the government introduced a bill and passed legislation ordering them back to work.
I am not going to discuss the sorry results of the government's decision, Mr. Speaker. I am not going to discuss whether the government should have known that the postal workers would not obey the law immediately and go back to work. Whether the government gave consideration to that, I do not know, but on the first day the workers in the post office went on strike the government brought in legislation to end it.
I said on that day, and I repeat, that if a government believes there is any group of workers whose service is so important they cannot be permitted to strike, then the government should pass legislation along that line. Workers have the same rights as other citizens to know what the rules of the game are; they ought not to have the rules changed in the middle of the game.

The bill before us tonight flows from a dispute between two unions of workers and the companies, the Canadian Lake Carriers Association. They went through the process of collective bargaining and could not reach an agreement, so the government appointed a conciliator who made a recommendation that the workers should receive an increase of 10'/5 per cent in the first year, and that in the second year they should get an increase of 2 per cent plus whatever the cost of living increase is in that year.
I suggest to members of the House that this is not an exorbitant amount. After all, the cost of living in the past year has gone up by almost 10 per cent. There is no indication that the increase in the cost of living will lessen in the next year. The only people arguing that are those on the Anti-Inflation Board who have consistently been wrong for the last two years. That being the case, the workers and their unions were not asking for too much when they asked for this kind of increase over the next two years. The conciliator was not being overly generous when he made that recommendation.
What happened? Did the Lake Carriers Association reject that proposal because they could not afford it, their customers could not afford it or their profits were too low? No. The Lake Carriers Association clothed themselves in a cloak of virtue and said they would not agree to the conciliator's recommendation because it would be inflationary.
1 have never heard of a company stating that it would not increase the price of its product because to do so would be inflationary. Bank profits went up all through the period in which we had the so-called anti-inflation program. In fact, they went up between 20 per cent and 25 per cent a year. The paper companies are reaping unprecedented profits, thanks in large part to the devalued Canadian dollar. Their profits are enormous. Have they decided to hold their price because they are already making enough money? No, Mr. Speaker, they increased their price very substantially. At the same time, their workers were forced to accept a relatively low increase in wages because the anti-inflation guidelines would not permit a larger increase.
I want to point out an interesting fact. One paper company that is showing remarkable profits is Consolidated Bathurst. It has reaped the benefits of increased prices. This has resulted in a very large increase in their profits. Consolidated Bathurst is controlled by Power Corporation, the president of which is Paul Desmarais. Wearing his hat as head of Consolidated Bathurst, Mr. Desmarais does not hesitate to raise the price of paper. However, wearing his hat as head of Canada Steamship Lines, he says they cannot agree to the increase which the conciliator has recommended because it would be inflationary. That is a very specious argument.
I am not surprised that we are having the difficulties we are. I do not have any inside information. However, it should be obvious that in the next year or two this country will have a series of strikes the likes of which we have never seen before. The workers of this country will not agree to a 6 per cent
October 23, 1978

increase, which is what the government proposes, while the cost of living is going up by between 9 per cent and 10 per cent.
To do that voluntarily would be agreeing in advance to a reduction in their standard of living. The workers of Canada will not make that sacrifice voluntarily if they are the only group in this country to do so. They are watching very carefully while corporation after corporation increases its prices and its profits and their standard of living is reduced.
We in principle do not like this kind of legislation. We believe that as part of the democratic system workers have the right to belong to unions and to bargain collectively. There has not as yet been devised a system which works better than the one in which workers have, as a last resort, the right to go on strike if they cannot settle their differences with their employers amicably.
The spokesman for the official opposition again today, as he has done on other occasions, said that there must be better ways. There are better ways. Other countries have tried other ways. Australia and New Zealand had a system of compulsory arbitration 50 years ago. It did not work too badly when the economy was relatively prosperous, when both employees and employers could agree on how to divide the benefits of the industry in which they were involved. However, that system broke down very seriously as soon as the economy went into a recession and it became obvious there were real differences between employer and employee.
We are therefore skeptical of any proposals made either in parliament or outside by academics or industrial relations experts with regard to systems which would supposedly work better than the one we have. Every citizen of Canada knows that when there is a strike, either in the private or the public sector, it hurts somebody. Workers do not go on strike easily. Like everyone else, they must earn a living. They need their weekly pay cheque to pay their bills.
Even when there is strike pay, and there usually is not, it is substantially less than a worker receives while on the job. Therefore, they do not go on strike frivolously. The proof is that more than 95 per cent of the negotiations which go on between union and employers result in a settlement without resorting to a strike.
We are opposed to legislation laying down procedures which prohibit a strike before it takes place. We are less than enthused about legislation which orders workers in the public or private sector back to work. I may disagree with the minister about whether or not he should bring in a bill. However, I am surprised when he brings in a bill which leaves the arbitrator to decide on the terms.
I do not know why the minister did not include the proposals of the conciliator in the bill. 1 believe they were reasonable. Possibly they are not acceptable to the companies. If the terms had been acceptable to the companies but not the union, I wonder whether they would have been included in the bill. With this minister, I believe they would have been. The reason they are not is that they are relatively favourable to the union.
Shipping Continuation Act
In the last week we have witnessed the beginning of a very serious trend in this country. We have witnessed the end of collective bargaining as we have known it. Some members will undoubtedly say that collective bargaining as we have known it does not work. I say it has worked in an overwhelming majority of cases. Those who say it is not working have yet to come up with a better system.
The government has known for months that there could be trouble in the post office, in the shipping industry and, I suppose, in other industries. Yet nothing was done; no effort was made to work out a policy which would be acceptable to the unions.
Let me say a word about what I take to be the implications of the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) on behalf of the official opposition. I do not believe for a moment one could get the co-operation of labour by setting up some sort of board or commission comprising some representatives of labour in the hope it would remove the necessity for strike action. Observers outside parliament who have discussed this question and compared Canada's record in the field of strikes and labour relations unfavourably with that of Sweden or Germany point to those countries and say that that is the way in which things should be done. But they take into consideration only one of the aspects having to do with strikes and labour-management negotiations. What they forget, or carefully omit to point out, is that in Sweden and Germany governments consult with the labour movement on all questions of economic and social concern to the ordinary people in those countries. They consult with the people with regard to obtaining full employment, measures dealing with inflation, the pension system and the social security system. They make labour a partner in the way government is run. In a similar fashion, they consult with industry.
This is never done in Canada. The only time labour is ever consulted is during a crisis when a group of workers in an industry to which the public is sensitive attempts to exercise its right under the law to go on strike. When that happens, the government gets into a panic and runs to labour with the plea: do something to stop this strike because it may be disastrous. Mr. Speaker, it may be disastrous in the short-run but it is a symptom of a deep-seated sickness which should have been dealt with much earlier. The government has never attempted to do this. It has never consulted with the workers or their unions with regard to any of the important questions which concern ordinary people.
Today, for the second time in a week we are presented with a bill ordering a group of workers to return to work though they are engaged in a legal strike. I do not know whether, when this legislation is passed, the government will have more success than it has experienced with the postal workers. I do not know what discussions are going on now, not only concerning this particular issue but concerning other and broader issues which affect workers in the shipping industry. I am not hopeful, because I see that the track record of the government

October 23, 1978
Shipping Continuation Act
is not good. They have gone to bat twice and they have struck out once and I am not at all sure they will not strike out a second time.
One of my hon. friends says the party opposite is an anti-labour party, and I am inclined to agree with him. I had always thought it was an anti-labour party but hon. members over there succeeded in disguising the fact. They are now showing themselves in their true colours. As they see it, the people who will be asked to bear the burdens of the ruinous economic policies they have followed for the last half a dozen or more years are the one million unemployed and the several million organized workers who do have jobs but who will be forced by legislation, or by whatever means the government can work out, to accept reductions in their real standard of living. That being the case I have no great hopes for the legislation before us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments on the bill the government introduced at six o'clock tonight. Hon. members are all fully aware of the fact that this House has repeatedly had to deal with bills of that type. As recently as last week, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) introduced a bill to provide for the resumption and continuation of postal services.
Mr. Speaker, introduction of such a bill surely proves one thing: that our labour legislation does not, by far, meet our current needs. It is unfortunate that the government has to resort to such procedures especially when it granted them the right to strike. Mr. Speaker, the introduction of this bill means that the government has recognized at last the urgency of the situation and the need to intervene to settle that problem which is as serious as the postal strike for all Canadians, especially the heavy losses that the Canadian economy could suffer in such conflict. However, as in the past, the government is unable to enforce the necessary measures.
In rising to speak on that bill, Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to blame the worker, on the contrary. We must blame the present economic system which is responsible for such problems. We only have to look around to note that strikes are increasing at a frightening speed. There was the recent strike of Air Canada flight personnel, we now have the postal conflict as well as the one we are discussing this evening and we will surely have others in a few weeks. I sincerely believe the government must take a stand in order to put an end to this dispute and take measures to avoid such situations in the future.
Mr. Speaker, it is no wonder that such strikes cause considerable losses to the Canadian economy, but do the workers have to take the blame for it? No, Mr. Speaker, that would be too simple. It would not solve the problem anyway because this is not the first time such things occur. On the contrary, we have been the victims of such breakdowns for years. The step the government has just taken by introducing this bill is likely

to allow our economy to function, more or less, for some time. I must also say the government should not limit itself to playing the part of a fire squad getting to the scene of a fire too late. The government must also be preventive. It must pass measures likely to eliminate the possibility of such situations.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the debate, I wonder if passing this bill will solve the problem we are facing now. As for me, I say no. Will that make the workers concerned go back to work? I doubt it. That, Mr. Speaker, will definitely not improve the situation, on the contrary it will only aggravate it. Let us take for example the acute problem in the Post Office after the passage of the legislation brought in last week by the the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, a bill to provide for the resumption and continuation of postal services. The union chose to challenge the law. Injunctions are being resorted to. We are witnessing civil disobedience, disorder, confusion, in short, anarchy!
I feel it is high time that the government take its responsibilities and see that the solutions advocated by my party for many years are adopted. Indeed, we the Social Credit Party of Canada are convinced that with our solutions the government would ensure greater co-operation between labour and management since in most cases workers resort to strike in order to get more purchasing power. When we realize that our government is now unable to control inflation, that inflation and salaries inci ,ase considerably while workers salaries increase slowly, there is no doubt about it. Strikes are the logical consequence of that situation. Mr. Speaker, before concluding, I would like to make three suggestions to the present government. First of all, I have a suggestion which would contribute to establish better relationships between employers and employees. It is a formula whereby the workers would share in the profits of the company, thus, enabling them to participate in the development of Canadian businesses.
Here is my second solution. For years, our party has been asking for the establishment of a permanent arbitration board with a power to make decisions without appeal. This board would consist of three arbitrators, the first being appointed by the employer, the second by the unions and the third by public authorities. Thanks to that regular and permanent mechanism it would be possible to achieve social peace in an orderly way, through the prevention of such conflicts even before they arise. That would eliminate the necessity of going before Parliament each time to pass a special legislation, which makes the right to strike inefficient and inoperative, and which leads to bandage solutions, as in the present case, when there are strikes and no settlements in sight; this only serves to widen the gap between workers and employer, which tomorrow maybe too wide to fill.
I would therefore offer a third solution, Mr. Speaker. I seriously believe that the guaranteed minimum income and compensated discount formula, put forth and defended by my party for many years, would greatly help in solving such
October 23, 1978

problems because that formula would allow workers in general to increase their wages without influencing prices, since we live in a vicious circle where inflation forces workers to resort to strike action if they are denied the increases asked for through normal channels.
I therefore believe, Mr. Speaker, that the present government should take its responsibilities and react as a good government should. It should apply the theories of the Social Credit Party of Canada as regards the cost of living and labor management relations and that would certainly restore social peace among our people.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to say a few words about the bill which has been brought into the House tonight. 1 can understand the absence of the Acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet).

speechtext:
Oh, he is back. I know that he is a busy minister because this is the second time in less than a week that we have this kind of legislation before us, which tells us that the government is incapable of dealing with the collective bargaining process, whether it be in the public sector or in the private sector. I do not know if I should say I am happy because it means a cost to taxpayers, but I see bureaucrats from the Department of Labour here tonight making all kinds of overtime.
It is interesting that once again we are dealing with back to work legislation. This time it is not in the public sector but in the private sector, and I wonder how this government will handle some of the problems which will arise after putting this kind of legislation into effect.
Even now as I stand here the government has its injunctions in the postal dispute in Halifax and Montreal, but the police forces in those places are refusing to serve them. I wonder how the government will solve that kind of problem once it has passed this back to work legislation. It seems to me that there are shades of 1919 all over again. I suppose we will have to get the RCMP to get out their horses. The RCMP will now enforce the law. The lawbreakers will enforce the law. Over the next couple of weeks there will be an interesting kettle of fish to observe.
I cannot help but comment on the sanctimonious and phony attitude of members of the official opposition. They talk much about bringing in the Woods committee report. The Woods
Shipping Continuation Act
committee report is nothing but a dressed up compulsory arbitration program. It certainly is not a recognition of free collective bargaining.
Here we are tonight putting marine engineers back to work, and we wonder who will be next. What will be the next thing to be declared an essential operation? Who is going to be declared essential? I suspect that every occupational group could be considered essential. After two days of a garbage strike garbage collection is very essential. If certain services are essential, then it seems to me there should be some process of free collective bargaining long before parliament puts workers back on the job.
It seems to me that this habit is becoming very regular. It is the second time in a week. Surely the whole question of free collective bargaining, the notion of bargaining in good faith, will be thrown out the window by employers in the private sector if they get the impression that parliament is prepared to step in and put workers back to work the minute they set off on a strike. There is not an evening that I turn on the TV set to watch the news that I do not hear of a strike here and a strike there. It shows the irresponsibility of the media, both print and electronic, when all that is ever reported is strikes. They never report the fact that 95 per cent of all collective bargaining ends in an amicable solution, that in effect only a small number of processes end by way of the strike route.
The question must be raised, and it must be raised squarely. Here are workers who two and a half years ago were accused of putting Canada into an uncompetitive position with respect to trade in the world. Workers were dumped on in this country and blamed for causing inflation. We were all aware of Gallup polls and all sorts of other polls which said that the problem with the economy of Canada is big trade unions, then big government, and somewhere after Idi Amin came big corporations. There was a bias, catered to by the two big parties, the Liberals and the Conservatives, at both the federal and provincial levels, which dumped on labour, dumped on the working class in this country, so that even workers started blaming each other for the economic mess in which we find ourselves.
Under this guise the government brought in wage controls and for two years they controlled the workers' wages. While they controlled wages and held them to an average increase of 6 per cent, when corporate profits were increasing at an average of 16 per cent, they did not do a very good job of controlling corporate profits. But they sure as hell controlled workers' wages. So whom do they blame now because the inflation rate is as high as it was at the time when the controls were brought in? They blame the public sector employees. They are not going to be the lead dogs. We saw a great program launched by this government saying in effect that the government would not allow public sector employees in this country to be the lead dogs for increases in the private sector. But when you examine the facts, you find that in comparing positions in the public sector with those in the private sector, in every single instance-we are not talking about the level of

October 23, 1978
Shipping Continuation Act
deputy ministers-in the private sector wages are higher than in the public sector.
These are the facts, and yet this government continues to allow the public servants of this country to take it on the chin. It continues to treat them as scapegoats, which leads me to suspect that there is a Machiavellian plot in existence between the Bay Street boys, the corporate boys, and the front benches of this government, that somehow or other they will start an attack on the trade union movement, an attack on the collective bargaining process, and an attack on public sector employees.
The question then must be raised-and it is a legitimate one in my opinion-who will be next? Will it be the Inco workers? Will they be deprived of the right to free collective bargaining? That question has to be answered.
I must say that I find the official opposition to be very phony on this issue. They are trying to play super crotch on this issue. They are all for collective bargaining, but they are also for compulsory arbitration. It is like the definition of a lady of the night; she works both sides of the street. That is the kind of game they want to play; they want to work both sides of the street.
I heard the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) give a speech in Toronto in which he said we should remove the right to strike from the public sector. Yet all parties in the House, may I remind hon. members, voted to give public servants the right to strike. There was not a "nay" from the official opposition or from the government. They all agreed that the public sector should have that right. But the minute that the public service exercises the right to strike, lo and behold, after CUPW is on strike for only one day, this government shows how tough it is. It puts the workers back to work after only one day of strike.
It seems to me that the government has lost any rapport it had with the trade union movement in this country, and the official opposition is in no position, given the kinds of phony positions they take on labour issues in the House and in committees of the House, to engender in the trade union movement any sort of confidence that they are sensitive to the problems of the working class in this country. For example, they can never enter into a social contact with them, and that is one thing that distinguishes the group on this side of the House from groups on other sides of the House. They have no rapport with the working class.
Just last week I was in Windsor speaking to 500 members of the United Auto Workers, and I listened to the concerns those workers were expressing at the convention. They were concerned about plant closings, about technological change, about how it affected their employment, about the mobility of capital which could move them from a highly industrialized northern state to a southern state where right to work legislation and other kinds of anti-labour legislation are practised. Our workers were expressing the same concerns as well regarding the mobility of capital which permitted the moving of part plants from Canada to the southern United States and other countries abroad.
These are the concerns of our workers, but does the government come to grips with these concerns? Does it try in its legislation to give workers the right to negotiate technological change? No, it uses all sorts of little flimflam excuses and says: You cannot discuss technological change because you are under the PSSRA. These are concerns with which they have not come to grips. That we have the kind of mess that exists in terms of industrial relations in this country is because they do not understand and they are not sensitive to workers. The cabinet, the whole front bench, reads like a who's who from Bay Street.
When I look at those who want to replace them-one has just been elected in Ottawa Centre-we find that in that one case he was an adviser to Richard Nixon. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that that should give every worker a chill right up the back of his spine. These are the people who expect to be sensitive to labour in this country. No, sir, they will say to labour: "That is your place, boy. If you do not stay in your place, parliament will put you back to work."
I think they have embarked on a dangerous path. Tonight the government is faced with the situation of police forces in this country not carrying out the injunctions they have been told to carry out. So you have a law abiding group of citizens, 23,000 of them, who feel in their heart of hearts that they have to resort to civil disobedience. Why? Because the government has failed completely to deal effectively with the situation long before the strike took place. The government had 18 months in which to deal effectively with the problem in the post office, but it left it to the last minute. Then after one day of strike, the government turned around and brought in back to work legislation.
I cannot support in principle compulsory arbitration. It is a band-aid approach. It is a principle which will never be accepted by my party. It does not solve the problems down the road. In fact, we took the same position regarding the CUPW legislation. It takes away the right of workers to negotiate a solution to a particular problem. If parliament is prepared to jump in at the first sign that negotiations are breaking down, then free collective bargaining will be destroyed for the forsee-able future in Canada. It is a principle which is against the beliefs of the New Democratic Party.

If this type of legislation is used more often than absolutely essential, then it is not an exception to the rule but rather becomes the rule. In that event, all of those who are affected or involved in labour situations will have in the back of their minds that parliament will legislate their problems if agreement cannot be reached. The Acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Ouellet) has found a niche for which he is highly
Shipping Continuation Act
adapted. He should agree that this is an exception and not necessarily the rule.
We are plagued with the legislation which was passed a few days ago affecting the public service of Canada and the post office. Undoubtedly, Canadians are concerned about this. It has resulted in a bad situation because nothing was done except to force the workers back to work, thus removing the rights they would have under any other circumstances.
The situation before us here is a different one. I listened with interest to the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) who indicated that not much difficulty has resulted because of the short duration of the seaway strike, that shipments have been made to ports. No one will argue that this is not a critical situation; it is one which will have disastrous effects on the economy of the country. We depend on the export of raw materials, certainly wheat. Difficulties will develop in the entire agricultural industry if these elevators are not filled with grain, moved by water transportation instead of waiting for the winter months to fill them by rail transportation.
There is no argument about the fact that this is a critical situation that warrants consideration. It is my understanding that two unions were involved in this situation in the Great Lakes. Both unions went to conciliation. One union continued negotiations under the auspices of the Department of Labour; the other has arrived at a settlement. I would be interested in knowing why the second union has not been able to arrive at the same or a similar settlement. Our Acting Minister of Labour was involved in the negotiations concerning both these unions, but he has not bothered to tell parliament why there was a breakdown in negotiations on the part of one union or whether a similar type of agreement was offered to both. He has not given us the reason why the second union failed to come to an agreement.
The Minister of Transport and Minister of Justice told us earlier tonight that he wanted parliament to extend the term of the collective agreement for a period of approximately one year. A few minutes ago he said he wanted the term extended for two years, until 1981. I can only conclude that the agreement signed with one union was signed on the basis of a three-year term and we are now being asked to provide an agreement in terms of a three-year period for the other union.
If we extend the length of the contract we will obviously be saying to the members of that union, whatever the settlement may be, that it will not be for the period for which the union originally negotiated but will be extended an additional two years. That may have no appeal to hon. members of this House. I have listened to some of their speeches in the last couple of days, often with a great deal of disgust, and I am sure that most want to settle this strike, as they did a previous strike, and as they will probably want to settle a strike tomorrow by employees of Nordair, if such takes place, and the next day a strike by Air Canada and perhaps will want to settle every strike by legislation, not really caring what are the terms of the settlement.

October 23, 1978
Shipping Continuation Act
If that happens labour may decide that parliament is not being fair. Quite frankly parliament should not only be fair under the circumstances, it should be extremely generous. How many of us remember with some amazement the time when Lester B. Pearson was prime minister of this country and settled a strike by giving the union involved something like three times what that union anticipated getting? It was a number of years before another contract came back to this House for settlement because management decided this was a pretty dangerous way of settling labour disputes. That particular dispute also involved the seaway, and the settlement then was generous enough that we were not faced with this kind of legislation for a long time.
In the case of the postal workers we provided the basis and the framework for an agreement that extended the package for a period of one year, and then extended that for a period of two and a half years, without any added inducements. In fact, we allowed a participant to that dispute to go before the arbitrator and remove some of the things the union had already gained through an agreement it had negotiated. This was not covered in the Public Service Staff Relations Act. We allowed the government to go before its own arbitrator and take these things away.
The judge who has been appointed, as I understand the situation as a result of listening to the radio, has asked for a copy of the Public Service Staff Relations Act. He apparently had never seen it before. When he reads it and compares it with what we are now being asked to do, he will understand the reason for the government's intervention. He will understand why the government insisted on a strike in the postal workers case. The government would not agree with its employees on matters that really did not involve money. That judge may well make the decision that this parliament did not have the guts to make.
We are again being asked to negotiate an agreement, but not in respect of people in the public service, employees of Canada, but in respect of the employees of private industry, an industry which is not controlled in any way by parliament, except through regulation.
I am told that Mr. Desmarais has dinner at least once a week with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and perhaps as well with the Minister of Transport and others. Mr. Desmarais controls the Power Corporation and Great Lakes Shipping, or St. Lawrence Shipping or one of the other big shipping companies which carries out a large shipping operation through the seaway. I am not suggesting this has any bearing on the matter because maybe they do not talk about shipping at all.
In any event, we are now making a decision very much against the interests of the employees.
