speechtext:
Yes, it is very much against the interests of the employees. The strike resulted in a lock-out because the company would not agree to the conciliation board report, and it was a majority report. The report did not recommend any

great shake for the workers. It gave them a cost of living allowance for a period of one year, and suggested an increase of 2 per cent in the second year. That is not an extravagant package. I do not know the exact terms as the Acting Minister of Labour did not give them to us. He should have told us what they are as we are really negotiating this contract on behalf of a private industry and a union outside our control.
If we pass this bill we will have played a great role in this agreement because we will have extended it. The contract will run out in May, 1979, eight or nine months from now. The Minister of Transport originally wanted to extend this term until May, 1980. Now he wants it extended to 1981. So in effect we will be negotiating the term of that contract, and the length of any contract is a damned important thing. We should think about this. Do we really not care about the fact that we are forcing people to accept a contract even though they feel they have the right to strike? Do we really think these people should not have the right to strike simply because a strike will hurt the Canadian people and damage the nation's economy? Should we ask them to give up this right to strike because of that fact?
We are not asking them to do this, but rather we are imposing a limitation on their right to strike. In return for that lost right we should give these employees something worthwhile. We should be negotiating in their favour. Instead we are negotiating against them. The minister did not tell us what the original negotiation package included. He took part in the negotiations during the last few days so he must be aware of the contents. He should tell us what the negotiation package contained in order that we can be fully aware of what we are being asked to do in this arbitrary way. He did not do that.
We can only draw the conclusion that management caused this strike simply by saying that they would not agree to the majority report of the conciliation board. We take away from the company the right to lock the workers out. On the other hand, we stop the workers from getting the benefit of a collective agreement that is to their satisfaction by bringing in this legislation. It is very easy to change the date from 1978 to 1979 or from 1980 to 1981, but it means that those workers in this union will be dissatisfied in 1979, 1980 and 1981 because we have imposed on them our will and have not given them anything to lighten their burden.
We were told in the debate on Bill C-8 about all the merits of a mediator-arbitrator. In this piece of legislation-and this bothers me to no end-we are not passing a stereotype bill but a different one. Is it going to be different for every union we have to put back to work? I do not know how the government will word the legislation for Nordair next week when it decides that they have to fly. I am not sure whether it will fly as Air Canada or as an independent company, but just as sure as shooting, my friend from Hamilton will be asked by these two ministers to do something about solving the terrible transportation problem in Nordair.
October 23, 1978

It is very hard to know what the government will do in that case. Perhaps they will appoint a mediator or an administrator, which is a method that has not been used for some time. I remember when we put dockworkers back to work under the authority of an administrator. The government took over the workers, the docks and put an army in to run the industry. If the minister thinks that he will have trouble finding an arbitrator, he will have even more trouble finding an administrator who will look after financial responsibilities, the responsibilities of operating a union as well as a company, and the responsibility of overseeing all the people he will need to operate his office.
On several occasions I had the opportunity to have dinner with some of the administrators. Charlie Millard was one of the administrators of the docks or the seaway. Somebody was required to travel with the marine workers and pilots at all times under this system. It will be very difficult if we ever have to go to that level.
There is no argument with the fact that this situation has an influence on the economy of the country, but surely if you take away from a segment of the workers in this country the privileges they normally have and adopt new legislation because it is in the public interest, then you have an obligation to compensate those workers in some way. In this case we are not looking to compensate but to punish. What was done recently with the postal workers is, in my opinion, going to backfire very badly on the government and the administration of justice in this country. As my colleague has mentioned, if it results in the police being unwilling to enforce an injunction which is granted on an emergency basis, then we are in pretty bad shape.
Every member should be concerned about such legislation. It is all right to say that the socialists stand behind labour anyway whether they are right or wrong, but in this case hon. members as individuals, if they pass this bill, are passing judgment on what will happen to this union. If hon. members have any knowledge at all of collective agreements they will see that the extension by two years of the date of termination of this contract must play an important role in the outcome of this dispute.
I am not familiar with all the problems and difficulties involved in the discussions which were held with the Minister of Labour, but I think that he has an obligation to tell parliament what the outstanding differences are. It may well be that this House in its wisdom would see fit to implement some of those requests and deny others, but it would give to the workers a contract that would be for the period they anticipated. Then the workers can get back to moving wheat in the few weeks that are available before freeze-up.
We are not only making a settlement for that period in which we would like to ship the maximum amount of grain through the seaway to the terminal points, but we are making a decision that will be binding for the next three years. If the workers do not agree then it will lead to a great deal of conflict in the seaway over the next three years, Mr. Speaker. If you are going to take what people are asking for in a reasonable
Shipping Continuation Act
way-and this is a reasonable union which has not been involved in labour disputes over the years, one which has undoubtedly weighed very seriously its reasons for going on strike-plus the solutions already given to them by the conciliation board, water them down by establishing a mediator and expect it to carry in a labour agreement for a period of two or three years, you are all nuts.
The last point that I wish to mention is the matter of a mediator. We do not use the American arbitration system which has a panel of prominent Americans and Canadians who are available to unions which sign agreements providing that they accept at the conclusion of their contract compulsory arbitration or agreed arbitration. The panel is chosen from a group of Canadians or Americans who are available and who are agreed upon by both parties. We do not have such a panel. Arbitration in Canada is a very difficult and tedious task which quite often involves people who are not entirely familiar with the law. It is unfair that there has not been consultation between both parties as to the choice of an arbitrator-mediator, or whatever the person will be called. If the government were to indicate who they had in mind, both parties could provide input as to their choice. We may have legislated about ten or 12 cases in the past 20 years, but it seems to me that we have been very fortunate in most of the instances in providing a solution that was reasonable and acceptable and not particularly opposed by either side.
Because of the haste of the decision on the post office workers, I suggest we have developed the mental attitude in this place that we believe it is our responsibility and right at any time to impose on the workers of this country, whether in the public service or the private sector, the kind of settlement we believe to be in our interests while completely disregarding the interests of management and organized labour. If we carry that attitude to any degree of irresponsibility, we will reap in great measure the abuses we are heaping on the labour movement in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to follow up on the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South. My question is directed to the Acting Minister of Labour. He is very sensitive about the word "forthwith". In fact, he was quite insistent upon that word being included in Bill C-8, resulting in the mediator-arbitrator being appointed "forthwith". Has he received a definition from the Minister of Justice of the word "forthwith"? Once a precedent has been set in terms of appointing forthwith, one must assume that it has been dealt with at some length.
The minister will have to come up with something better than suggesting that he was boxed in. This bill indicates that an arbitrator can be appointed within hours, as did Bill C-8. What is the government's definition of "forthwith"? Is there flexibility within that definition? Will the minister accept an amendment to the bill to include the word "forthwith"? I think we should be consistent.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF SHIPPING SERVICES

If I am allowed, I should like to answer the hon. member in my mother tongue in order better to express my view on the definition of that word.

The word "forthwith" is defined in French as "immediate-ment" which means that, in fact, the Minister of Labour is obliged by law to appoint, as soon as possible, that is, immediately, a mediator-arbitrator, which is what I did in the case of the act requesting all postal employees to go back to work. As the definition and scope of the word can lead to confusion, it seemed preferable to me, in this bill, not to use the word and so allow the Minister of Labour to use his discretion that there might be no constraints or erroneous interpretation.
That is why, in the bill now before us, the word "forthwith" or "immediately" does not appear, which means that I have more latitude than in the previous bill, without it meaning however that I am allowed to shirk my responsibilities. On the contrary, I intend to use my prerogative as soon as possible.

That is one great story which I do not accept. Perhaps the Acting Minister of Labour is playing it cute right now. Bill C-8 was drawn up by the law officers of the Crown, and they found the word "forthwith" acceptable. If the minister wants to be consistent, that word should be included in the bill before us. Otherwise, it would mean that Bill C-8 is faulty.

Mr. Chairman, I am surprised that the Acting Minister of Labour could think this committee would complete dealing with this bill within a half hour and that the Senate could deal with it tonight. That is physically impossible. I have a number of matters that I want to raise, and I would like to raise them now so that the officials of the department may consider them in the hope constructive amendments may be made to a bill which I consider to be singularly deficient.
I am rather surprised at the NDP who seem to have abandoned ship, except for one caretaker over there. I guess that attitude was engendered after it was pointed out that the premier of Saskatchewan specifically asked for this type of legislation. Now they are silent.
There are several areas in the bill where the rights of workers are in jeopardy. It may have been sheer oversight because of the haste in which the legislation was drawn up, or it may display an attitude on the part of this government, namely that, notwithstanding their sanctimonious words about believing in collective bargaining and the rights of labour, they do not really believe in that at all.
It may display an attitude on the part of this government that, notwithstanding their sanctimonious words about believ-
Shipping Continuation Act
ing in collective bargaining and the rights of labour, they really do not believe it.
I point out to the government that, contrasted with the manner in which matters of this nature were dealt with by the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert, this legislation and the legislation for the Post Office completely negates any collective bargaining such as was, for instance, displayed in a bill introduced in December, 1960, which required the CNR to continue operating but at the same time required collective bargaining to continue. The caretaker here tonight for the New Democratic Party will remember that bill. Parliament dealt with the situation by continuing the collective bargaining process.
The Acting Minister of Labour has said that under this legislation the arbitrator will have to draft a collective agreement. He said that twice. But that is not my understanding of the legislation. I understand that matters in dispute between the parties are to be referred to the arbitrator, who then has to make a decision and that decision will constitute amendments to the existing agreement. There is no question of drafting a new agreement; all the arbitrator will do is amend.
One of the most disturbing features of the bill-and I hope the government will consider amendments in this area-is that the arbitrator is not required, by the legislation, to consult with labour or management either to determine the matters in issue between the parties or to hear from them with respect to how those issues are to be resolved. My understanding of the Post Office bill is that that process is followed and there is a right to be heard. In essence, this denial to both sides to be heard is a denial of the rules of natural justice, with which I am sure the Minister of Justice will be familiar although there have been occasions in the past when I doubted that. One of those was with reference to the prairie grain assistance act, where the statute used a term about paying the farmers, but the minister interpreted that as meaning no obligation to give those farmers any advance payment for wheat. There is a denial of natural justice here.
I suggest that the government examine clause 6. Surely, there should be incorporated in this clause the right of the parties to be heard before the arbitrator decides on the matter at issue. Clause 6(1 )(a), under which the minister appoints an arbitrator, gives that arbitrator power to decide what matters are to be decided by him. It makes no provision for input by the union or by management. It may be that there are issues not covered by the conciliation report that should be determined under this legislation. Input from both sides should be considered, and there should be input from both sides-within a strict time limit, if you will-providing the parties the right to be heard on those issues. Anything less than that is, surely, a denial of the rule of natural justice. It may be said that if we have that, it will lengthen the process and delay action under the bill. I suggest not, because clause 3 is quite explicit in requiring the shippers to ship and the workers to work until the decisions are made.
I agree with my colleagues who have raised the point about imposing a time limit within which the arbitrator is to be

appointed. Whether the word "forthwith" is used, or "immediately", I say a far more serious objection to imposing no time limit has been raised by my colleagues, because if one looks at clause 6(3) it appears that the arbitrator must make his decision on the matters at issue within 60 days after the date of the reference to him. It seems to me that any delay in appointing the arbitrator will reverberate all down the line. The postal bill used a 90-day term. I suggest a limitation period be laid down in this respect.
One does not have to use the word "forthwith". It could be two days, or five days, but a limitation should be placed on the appointment because that appointment triggers subclause 3 of clause 6.
The hon. member for Vegreville raised the point about reporting. That is clearly set out in the postal bill. In my opinion, this is one of the weakest clauses of the bill. Subclause 3 of clause 6 reads in part as follows:
-the arbitrator shall be required to decide all matters referred to him under this act within 60 days of his appointment.
My first observation concerns the words "be required . Required by whom? Does it require the minister's request before the arbitrator has to report? If not, why are those words there? Why could not it read, the arbitrator "shall decide all matters referred under this act within 60 days of his appointment"? Are the words superfluous, or do they require expanded explanation, placing an obligation on some minister to require that report?
With regard to clause 7(1), Mr. Chairman, one of the rules of natural justice respecting tribunals such as this-this might strike a chord in the memory of the Acting Minister of Labour-is that the report is in writing. There is no such requirement here. Another is that the report is made to a particular body and communicated to the parties. In this bill, we give power to the arbitrator to make decisions on matters that he deems to be at issue between the parties, without hearing the parties, and then a provision in the bill might require him to report. But even if he is required to report, to whom is the report to be made? Is it to the minister? There is no mention of that in the bill. Surely the arbitrator should be required to report to both union and management as a matter of course. I suggest it is the right of the parties to be informed of the decisions in writing.
A far more serious defect in the legislation occurs in the closing lines of subclause (1) of clause 7. If the whole of the clause is read, it will be seen that when the arbitrator decides all matters referred to him by the minister, the collective agreement to which this act applies is deemed to be amended by the incorporation of those decisions in the agreement and all such other amendments as are agreed upon by the parties prior to the decision of the arbitrator, and the collective agreement as so amended constitutes a new collective agreement. By clause 4 the agreement is extended to 1981. Subclause (2) of clause 4 makes it a collective agreement not

capable of future amendment if read in conjuction with subclause (1) of clause 7.
There is no way, even if the parties mutually agree, after the arbitrator's report that that collective agreement can be amended because the provisions of the Canada Labour Code are suspended by reading clause 4 and clause 7 together. That should be made clear so that the union and management are not denied the right to come to mutually agreed upon amendments after the arbitrator makes his decision. That is certainly not in the legislation now. Again, that is a very serious deficiency in the bill.
We on this side of the House are in full accord with the expression of the laws contained in clause 3. We have to get shipping moving and the workers back to work. However, when one looks at clause 8 and clause 9 and compares them with the law on injunctions, a subject matter about which the minister may still remember a few principles, one will see that there are very serious deficiencies indeed.
First, it is my submission to the government that clause 8(1) divests the court of any discretion in the matter of granting an injunction. As a personal viewpoint, I will concur with the approach that the Federal Court, upon a proper application being made, shall be required to issue an injunction. However, surely the terms upon which the court issues that injunction are still a matter of discretion for the court. Not so by clause 8 of this legislation. The injunction shall-and that is a mandatory term-be granted, and it shall direct any company or union to comply with the provisions of this act. That is all.
It shall also be a provision that they may be cited for contempt of the injunction and punished as contempts are usually punished. Surely there should be a provision in that clause that the court shall issue an injunction upon such terms as the court may deem just. That discretion should reside in the judicial bodies that we have set up throughout the country for the purpose of safeguarding the rights and liberties of all.
By permitting the legislation to remain in these terms, you take that discretion away from the court. I see the minister shaking his head, indicating that that is not the intention. I am not accusing the government of saying that it was their intention, but that is the effect of that clause. The jurisdiction is mandatory in the sense that the court may grant an injunction only in the terms set out in clause 8, and none other.

All of these cases are not referred to the House of Commons. It is only some specific and particular cases which are referred to parliament.
It has been the philosophy of the current government that when an individual right becomes a public wrong, the government faces its responsibility squarely. It does not hide behind any labour tribunal or public interest dispute tribunal that might be proposed. Parliament is asked to accept its responsibilities and terminate this dispute. However, I agree with the hon. member that this recourse should not be abused. I think it is illogical to believe that some group, some tribunal or some public interest dispute tribunal could solve the problem. I do not think we can consider such a solution. I think that basically we must believe in the due process of collective bargaining, and only on special occasions should we ask parliament to intervene, as we are forced to do today. In Canada we are faced with problems related to the grain handlers, engineers and skippers on the Great Lakes, and to the general work force. My question is directed to the Minister of Transport and the Acting Minister of Labour. We have reached a point where we are creating in Canada today a growing number of terribly dissatisfied male and female workers. For example, millions of dollars can be put into job creation, but millions of dollars cannot be put into job happiness.
Usually, we in this House can enjoy our job, work five days a week here and then go home and do the things we want to do on weekends. We look after the things under our control as members of parliament while we are here, and we assume that the people who have to fill the ships, fill the hopper cars and look after the transportation system are able to do the same thing.
What is really fundamental is that we in this chamber, which is the most powerful legislative chamber in this country, do everything we can to make work more meaningful for the people of this country. Perhaps I am saying the wrong thing, and maybe I am even out of order.

We have an opportunity tonight, and every day, to humanize the work of the working force in this country. Unless we, as the elected members of parliament, attempt once again to humanize work, we will be failing in our responsibilities.
Many members, over there, as well as on this side, did all kinds of jobs when we were young; and unless we do something

to humanize those kinds of jobs, we will be in trouble. Let me give a few examples. You can go to the assembly line at Massey-Ferguson in Brantford and see the kind of work I have in mind. I worked for a steamship line for a number of years as a short-order cook. That was a human job at that time, but today it is not. I worked on a section gang for the CNR. That was a very important job in those days. We are losing the demand for and the responsibility involved in that kind of a job, and we are losing respect for an honest day's work.
What are hon. members on the other side of the House doing to rehumanize the idea of a good day's work? What are hon. members over there trying to do, in real terms, to bring humanity back to the work force? What they are doing is buying more computers, more mechanical aids and more machines. This is what we are talking about tonight. We are talking about people; we are not talking about a bill. Bills come and go, but we are talking about human beings. It is about time the Minister of Transport and the Acting Minister of Labour, wherever he is now, started to think in terms of human beings in this country, rather than numbers. We should be talking in terms of human beings, rather than social insurance numbers and income tax numbers. We are talking about people, and it is about time we in this House started to think in terms of human beings, rather than in terms of numbers. I do not know whether I have asked a question.

subtopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT-LEGISLATION TO AMEND- LEVEL OF PENSION FOR WIDOWS OF DISABLED VETERANS

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT-LEGISLATION TO AMEND- LEVEL OF PENSION FOR WIDOWS OF DISABLED VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not blame those members who are leaving, since it is now 12.47 a.m. However, I want to express my pleasure that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) is here. He agreed to stay tonight to whatever hour it might be to answer the question that I put down for this adjournment debate.
My question arises from a two-part inquiry that I put to the Minister of Veterans Affairs on Tuesday, October 17, 1978, as

recorded in Hansard for that date at page 165. The first part of my question had to do with the announced review of the War Veterans Allowance Act. The second part had to do with the question of pensions for widows of disabled veterans, those pensions coming under the Pension Act.
With regard to the War Veterans Allowance Act, I can say that all of us who are interested in veterans pensions welcomed the announcement the minister made during the last session that this act was being reviewed.
It can be said that in the last number of years we have made a good many amendments to the Pension Act and, in effect, we have made many improvements in the provisions under that legislation. While we have been doing that, not much has been done to the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I could remind hon. members that the War Veterans Allowance Act was brought before parliament in the early 1930s. Its purpose at that time was to provide for veterans who did not qualify under the Pension Act under which pensions for disability are paid, something a little better than was available to the civilian population under the then old age pensions act.
I should remind the minister and others that over the years-we are talking about a period of 47 or 48 years-a great many changes have been made in pension legislation, especially for the population generally. The result is that the provisions for veterans and their survivors under the War Veterans Allowance Act are no longer much better than are available to civilians generally. One of the main differences, of course, is that the means test which applied to the old age pension back in the thirties and which was therefore carried over to the War Veterans Allowance Act no longer applies to the basic amount of the pension under the Old Age Security Act. This is one aspect which it seems to me should be looked into. I feel strongly that the time has come, so many years after the wars in which our veterans have participated, for there to be a form of guaranteed annual income for veterans at a certain age and that we would be doing a service both to veterans and to our pension legislation by abolishing a good deal of the red tape and the obstacles that are now in place.
These are just a few thoughts I offer about the War Veterans Allowance Act. I appreciate the minister's answer that when he gets the result of the review he will make suggestions about what should be done. I hope his decision will result in legislation this session, or, if action is not possible right away, in a reference to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
The other part of my question referred to the remaining issue in the Pension Act, the fact that when a veteran dies, if his disability pension was below 48 per cent there is no pension for his widow. We have been over this back and forth. I know all the arguments the minister can use in defence of the present position, but he knows too, particularly as the veterans of World War II are getting older, that this becomes more and more a matter of deep concern to them, and I do not think that our so-called veterans' legislation, our so-called veterans'
October 23, 1978

charter, will be what it ought to be until we resolve this issue, at least to the extent of providing pro rata pensions for widows where the veteran's pension was below 48 per cent.
We have done well in getting the pension rate attached to a standard of wage in the public service. We have done well in getting a certain amount of compensation for prisoners of war both in World War II and World War I. We have done well in many of the things we have achieved with respect to veterans' legislation, and I refer now in particular to the Pension Act. However, this shortcoming still exists, and while I appreciate the fact that the other day the minister's answer seemed to imply some active consideration of the review of the War Veterans Allowance Act, he did not seem very hopeful that he would be bringing in something in this session to provide these pro rata pensions for widows where the veteran's disability pension was below 48 per cent.
I suggest to the minister that this parliament still has a number of months to go, probably into next spring or next summer, and when that time comes, it will not be good enough for the minister or for those on his side of the House to talk about what was done for veterans in the last few years. The question will be what was done in this session.
To sum up these remarks tonight, I say to the minister that what ought to be done, what the veterans would appreciate, would be to make a substantial improvement in the War Veterans Allowance Act and to amend the Pension Act to provide pro rata pensions for widows where the veteran's pension was below 48 per cent.
I hope the minister can say something encouraging. I do not expect him to announce tonight that something will be brought in tomorrow, but I hope he will tell us that these two matters will be given serious attention and consideration during this session.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE ACT-LEGISLATION TO AMEND- LEVEL OF PENSION FOR WIDOWS OF DISABLED VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, staff of the Department of Veterans Affairs have over the past year been conducting a fundamental review of the War Veterans Allowance Act and part XI of the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. During the review a detailed evaluation is to be carried out on how well the legislation meets its objectives, both in the nature and level of benefits provided to the veteran, dependants and survivors, as well as in the ways and means of determining and delivering the benefits. The examination was undertaken as a result of our recognizing, first, that the age and circumstances of the veteran and family today are very different from 1930 when the legislation was created, and second, that the methods used to administer the legislation might no longer be the most appropriate. The review is to focus on identifying opportunities for improving benefits to recipients and streamlining the administration of such benefits.
The review is reaching the stage where a report on the evaluation findings and a preliminary identification of alternative methods of achieving the objective of the legislation is due.
Adjournment Debate
This will not be a final document; rather, it will be a progress report permitting guidance to be given on the general direction the study should take during its concluding phases.
The question of paying pro rata pensions to widows of pensioned veterans has been raised by the hon. member many times. It has been suggested that a widow should receive a pro rata pension if her husband had been in receipt of a disability pension assessed at the rate of 47 per cent or less. Had his pension been assessed at the rate of 48 per cent or more, the surviving dependants would be pensionable. It should be remembered that a widow will be pensioned if her husband's death was attributable to service or occurred during wartime, regardless of the degree of the assessment of the disability.
I can assure the hon. member that when I have something specific to report on either of these subjects, I shall be pleased to do so.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR CONTINUATION OF ESQUIMALT AND NANAIMO RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR CONTINUATION OF ESQUIMALT AND NANAIMO RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather a shock for me to find myself speaking on an adjournment debate at two minutes to 1 a.m., but the subject is important. It arises out of a question I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on October 20 about the Esquimalt-Nanaimo railway. I asked him if he could assure Vancouver Islanders that this popular, and now profitable, rail service will continue beyond December 13. The minister gave me more than the usual favourable answer and told me he presumed that the remarkable increase in the number of people using the services will be taken into account in the various steps which have to be taken with regard to the future of the rail service.
This story goes back a considerable distance. It is a long story of the CPR attempting to abandon a railway that is providing passenger service, and I am sure it has happened in other cases in the country. In this case the Canadian Transport Commission in 1970 and 1973 denied the railway the petition to abandon service and ordered some improvements to take place in the promotion of the service, station improvements and provision of sufficient equipment so that they could avoid carrying passengers in the baggage section.
These ordered improvements were given no attention or minimal attention by the railway, and in fact the line deteriorated so much that the northern section had to be closed in 1975. The railway attempted to avoid necessary repairs for reopening the line. The Canadian Transport Commission ordered that the line be repaired, and it was reopened in December, 1977.
From then on it was the story of the railway trying to give such poor service that nobody would use it and the railway could use that as an excuse to close down the line. Fares were prohibitively high, much higher than bus fares and CPR fares in other places, such as from Calgary to Red Deer. The only promotional effort was the printing of a few time cards. The

October 23, 1978
Adjournment Debate
stations were in disrepair, often locked. Passenger inquiries had no local phone number on the island to phone for information. No food service was available, not even vending machines in either the train or in the stations. The Victoria terminal was relocated away from the city in an inaccessible suburban location. Permanent slow orders were in effect, delaying the train on every trip, without any public notification of the later schedule; thus trains were chronically and permanently behind time. No Sunday service was available, a day which has proven to be one on which there is heavy demand for service.
Predictably, the number of passengers was reduced to the very few who somehow discovered the existence of the service and could afford the exorbitant rate. The railway was given permission to discontinue service, although a one year extension of the order was granted to allow for appeal. This period expires on December 13 this year.
Local residents aware of the significant need and market demand for the service which existed have realized that they must use the service, despite the existing glaring deficiencies. Since December, 1977, thanks to an ad hoc committee which was formed by Mr. John Cooper and Mr. Win Moss to support the railway, loadings have climbed steadily to become impressive indeed. By May, loadings were regularly exceeding the capacity of the single unit available. By June the average daily loadings for the month exceeded 100 per cent of the seating capacity.
In summary, instead of the previous 8,000 to 12,000 passengers per year of recent years, this year saw loadings of over 40,000, and this in spite of the deficiencies in the service.
CPR has responded to the increased demand for service in a minimal way. The CPR action to fight against this ad hoc committee increasing the number of passengers carried has been as follows. No timetables have been available for over four months. Since this is the only company promotion for the service, it does not seem unreasonable to expect timetables, especially in view of changes in the service and fares. Slow orders keeping the train at 30 miles per hour were lifted only after public pressure. Stations have been unlocked after public pressure. Extra equipment has been added only after intense public pressure and the offer to help from B.C. rail.
Sunday service has been added but only after public pressure. After six weeks it was retained because of additional public pressure. Timetables and posters printed by an island daily and by private subscription were removed from the stations and train by order of the company, even though no timetable exists. The Canadian Pacific Railway feels no obligation toward persons who cannot board trains due to overloads, except on occasion to post signs in stations of high-use days warning potential passengers against using the train.
The new, substantially cheaper VIA fares were introduced only after they had been introduced throughout the rest of Canada first, and then only after public pressure. VIA excursion fares were not introduced until some six weeks later, when public pressure brought the matter to light. Amenities are

minimal: stations have no phones; the on-board ash trays are used salmon tins; the disposal kit is an old bucket; the toilets are consistently out of order; and no on-board food service of any kind is available.
These items stress two facts. The CPR has provided service grudgingly, poorly, and only when subject to public pressure and scrutiny on a constant basis. The public response to the service, in light of the foregoing facts, underlines the very real need for the service. Certainly no one is riding because it offers luxury accommodation.
The present schedule is not adequate. It would be much more efficient to use a two-car train which each day would travel from Victoria to the north end of the island and back. One car at each end could be started at the same time. They are self-propelled. They could cater to northern Vancouver Island citizens, as well as the citizens of Victoria and its environs.
At the present time it is not possible for the railway to take this on, because there is an outstanding appeal by the British Columbia provincial government and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). But it is my understanding that the minister can authorize an extension of the present extension for another five years, and I ask him to do that. It would give VIA Rail time to get firm control of the passenger service on that railway. Also it would provide the time necessary to continue developing the services on the island. If the minister gives the additional five years, we are confident that the railway will be made permanent and profitable.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR CONTINUATION OF ESQUIMALT AND NANAIMO RAIL PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has just raised a problem that several members of this House have experienced in the past and will probably experience in the future. It concerns the fact that our railroads, whether Canadian National or Canadian Pacific, have too often in the past neglected passenger services for more profitable services. In fact, this is why the government established VIA Rail so as to put some order in passenger services and attempt to serve the Canadians who need these services to travel from place to place as they deserve.

As the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) points out, patronage has increased on this service over the past years as a result of the publicity generated about the service and the introduction of fare reductions this past summer. In June and July, patronage was up 130 per cent over the same period last year, and average loads during this period were around 78 persons per trip. Accordingly, on July 28, 1978, Canadian Pacific added an additional car to the train, thereby increasing capacity from 71 seats to 161 seats each way. Canadian Pacific reports that overloads have occurred only on a few weekends due to groups arriving at the station which are larger than had been indicated earlier to agents. September 30 and October 9 were two dates cited.
October 23, 1978

I should note that the president of VIA Rail inspected the facilities personally last week in order to assess problems with the current service. The Canadian Transport Commission, in its evaluation of this service, determined that it is uneconomic, and a good quality road network and bus service parallels the railway between Victoria and Courtenay. These reasons contributed to the CTC decision to allow the discontinuance.
